article_text:
C’est le premier long métrage de Marine Atlan. Qu’est-ce qui, dans le scénario, vous a donné envie d’embarquer ?

Le scénario m’a fait une très forte impression parce qu’il a une qualité littéraire assez exceptionnelle, une épaisseur, une étoffe. Marine est aussi chef opératrice. Et donc il y avait déjà une description de l’opération de la lumière sur les corps, du rapport, très présent dans le film, entre la lumière et les ténèbres, qui est très propre aussi à la culture du sud de l’Italie, avec le Caravage, le ténébrisme, tout ça. Il y avait déjà, rien qu’à l’écrit, dans le scénario, une dimension comme ça dans l’estrade temporelle, dans l’épaisseur du silence, dans le rythme.

J’étais très impressionnée aussi par la trajectoire de Mercier, un personnage qui se déploie de façon assez riche. C’est un parcours hyper riche dans la mesure où on est en même temps avec une figure d’enseignante dans tout ce qui a trait à l’exercice de son métier, c’est-à-dire faire des cours, essayer de transmettre vraiment un savoir, de mobiliser les jeunes, de capter leur attention, de les amener à traverser eux-mêmes ce récit initiatique de l’adolescence et à s’éveiller à une autonomie. Il y a toute cette ferveur-là. Et puis, en même temps, c’est une femme qui est à un certain stade de sa vie, qui a peut-être une forme de désillusion ou un sentiment parfois de ne pas exercer son métier dans les bonnes conditions, et qui a aussi une part de mélancolie très forte.

Bref, tout ça pour dire que déjà, à la lecture, c’est quelque chose que j’ai perçu de manière en même temps consciente et en sentant que, chez l’autrice, Marine, et sa co-autrice Anne Brouillet, il y avait une espèce de point de contact poétique, intime, qui me reliait à leur travail. J’avais absolument envie que cette rencontre ait lieu.

▌ À LIRE AUSSI

Marine Atlan : « J’ai traversé des choses assez profondes de mon histoire avec La Gradiva »

Il y a une grande tension qui se dégage de Pompéi, le décor du film. Est-ce que ça a joué un rôle dans votre jeu ?

Absolument, parce que les sites en question, la cartographie des décors et du trajet que font les personnages, ce sont des signifiants hyper puissants. Ce sont des lieux qui activent, qui agissent, qui ont eu une histoire et qui ont aussi une dimension géologique, tellurique. Il y a une puissance. Et le fait qu’on ait beaucoup travaillé en amont, beaucoup répété, a permis d’arriver sur ces sites et de pouvoir ensuite les traverser. Je pense à la Villa des Mystères, par exemple. C’est très impressionnant d’être face à une fresque qui a été enfouie pendant 2 000 ans et qui est dans un état de conservation exceptionnel parce que, du fait de la catastrophe de l’éruption du Vésuve, elle a été enfouie, donc préservée de l’action de l’air ou de la lumière. D’être face à son éclat et à son état de conservation, impeccable.

Le fait d’avoir travaillé en amont à Paris le rapport que Mercier peut établir avec ses élèves, l’écosystème de la classe, le climat d’une classe, et la manière dont l’autorité, ou en tout cas le travail de pédagogue, s’exerce, ça nous a permis, une fois là-bas, d’être vraiment en prise avec cette dimension du vertige. Et avec cette dimension de ces lieux, de leur héritage, même de manière confuse : c’est un héritage collectif hyper puissant, et ce sont aussi des territoires avec une forme de dangerosité. Pompéi, ce sont clairement les vestiges d’une tragédie. Et le Vésuve, c’est ce volcan qui continue à menacer Naples, la baie de Naples et les habitants aux alentours. Ce sont des sites chargés, qui ont un rapport à la mémoire, qui ont un rapport à la mort. D’ailleurs, le titre, « La Gradiva », raconte vraiment ça.

Qu’est-ce qu’il raconte ?

Ça vient d’une nouvelle d’un auteur allemand qui s’appelle Janssen, qui avait écrit l’histoire d’un archéologue qui trouve un bas-relief, une sculpture d’une femme qui marche, et il commence à la délirer, à la fantasmer. Ensuite, il la voit à Pompéi avant l’éruption du Vésuve. Il y a vraiment toute une affabulation autour de cette figure. Freud en fera un commentaire plus tard, et il fait une analogie que je trouve hyper intéressante et qui raconte vraiment quelque chose du film. C’est une analogie entre le refoulement, qui est une part psychique inaccessible mais qui, du fait même qu’elle est inaccessible, est conservée quelque part en nous, et la ville de Pompéi, qui a été enfouie : il y a aussi cet état de conservation. Il dit que l’archéologue et le psychanalyste ont ce même travail d’excaver, pour déterrer soit une civilisation enfouie antique, soit un désir infantile enfoui.

L’Italie regorge de mythes liés à des hallucinations, la beauté fantomatique des lieux mais aussi un bouillonnement social. Qu’avez-vous ressenti sur le tournage ?

À Naples, il y a un effet d’enchevêtrement iconoclaste : il y a 2 000 ans d’histoire, il y a en même temps des espèces de collages, des alliances inédites entre Maradona et les églises, qui se multiplient sur le territoire. Et puis tu passes dans une rue, tu rentres dans une église et il y a les Sept Œuvres de la miséricorde du Caravage à portée de main. En même temps, quand on lit Saviano [ Roberto Saviano, écrivain et journaliste italien, qui s’attaque dans ses livres aux milieux mafieux, ndlr ], par exemple, c’est un lieu qui est aussi un épicentre des problématiques contemporaines, du capitalisme forcené, du tourisme de masse, de la mafia qui a réussi à récupérer les rouages du capitalisme pour s’infiltrer dans la société. Il y a un foisonnement assez impressionnant, qui peut être un peu écrasant aussi.

Votre interprétation est très intense, physique…

Oui, il y a une ferveur, une foi. Pour être enseignant, je pense qu’il faut une croyance dans cette transmission des savoirs, dans le fait de convoquer les élèves et, encore une fois, de les amener à être autonomes et critiques. Ça tient à cette volonté de vitaliser le cours. C’est en ça qu’un enseignant, une enseignante, est vraiment un chef d’orchestre.

Et chez Mercier, tout cet engagement physique, pour moi, il racontait en même temps sa ferveur, mais aussi peut-être son impatience. C’est presque le revers de la même médaille : autant on anime les choses en s’y engageant pleinement pour faire advenir des images, des savoirs, des histoires, autant, si ça s’arrête, il y a quelque chose de l’expérience de la perte, de la vacuité, qui est tout aussi immédiat. C’est comme si son animation lui permettait de lutter contre le vide, de lutter contre un découragement.

Oui, car le dynamisme de Mercier cohabite avec une grande mélancolie. Comment comprenez-vous cette dualité-là ?

J’avais lu un truc sur Béla Tarr qui disait que, pour lui, la mélancolie, c’était avoir le sentiment de perte avant même de perdre l’objet. Et j’ai l’impression que c’est peut-être aussi l’intransigeance, l’exigence qu’a Mercier vis-à-vis de Toni [ le personnage principal du film, incarné par Colas Quignard, ndlr ]. C’est peut-être parce qu’il y a une forme de reconnaissance. On parlait de la ferveur de Mercier et de ce moment où, si ça s’arrête, on fait l’expérience du rien. De la même façon, Toni décuple ses capacités d’inventivité, d’énergie pour générer de la lumière. Il a cette part radieuse, et en même temps on voit aussi toute la part dans laquelle il bascule et il sombre. Ça communique, ces points paroxysmiques.

▌ À LIRE AUSSI

NOUVELLE STAR · Colas Quignard : « J’aime le fait d’être dirigé, de devoir saisir où on veut m’emmener, d’essayer et de me tromper. »

Il y a un moment où le film peut faire un peu peur, quand il s’engage sur une soirée que passent ensemble James, l’un de ses élèves, et Mercier et qui semble lentement dériver. On sent poindre une ambiguïté entre eux, puis le film retombe sur ses pattes. Comment avez-vous compris cette séquence ?

Absolument. On peut la comprendre différemment, comme toujours. Beaucoup de gens m’ont parlé du fait qu’ils avaient eu peur et qu’ils étaient très rassurés qu’il ne se passe finalement rien. Ils comptaient sur Mercier pour que ça ne se passe pas !

Ce que j’ai compris de ça, c’est qu’il y a pour moi une scène pivot en amont de l’évasion, du chemin de traverse que vont prendre Mercier et James à travers les ruines de Naples : c’est la scène au musée archéologique. Là, chaque personnage est comme dans une grande scène théâtrale où le drame serait un peu joué d’avance. Il y a quelque chose d’un peu déchu, ils sont tous renvoyés à leur solitude, à leur honte, à leur dégoût, dans cette déambulation avec ces œuvres figées, autoritaires, impressionnantes. À partir de là, il y a cette scène de simulation d’un carnage orchestré par Suzanne, et il y a quelque chose qui se dérègle.

Et l’évasion, ce que je vois comme cette espèce de sortie de champ, presque une sortie de sa mission de professeur avec James, pour moi, ce n’est pas de l’ordre du trouble vraiment érotique ou sexuel, ou d’une attirance réelle. C’est plus un ébranlement. À ce moment-là, il y a un ébranlement généralisé et c’est aussi, tout d’un coup, laisser un peu d’espace à un élan vers autre chose. On pourrait se dire qu’elle est au paroxysme de son enjeu de pédagogue, en lui parlant de tout ce qu’ils voient autour d’eux, dans une espèce de partage privilégié avec lui. Et en fait, il ne se passe pas grand-chose. C’est une sorte de transgression, mais qui fait apparaître la limite. C’est Georges Bataille qui le dit : la transgression fait apparaître la limite. Et il y a quelque chose qui arrête cette espèce de divagation, de digression.

En tout cas, je pense que c’est très bien qu’elle récupère une place de professeur, et qu’un temps, peut-être, elle ait pu penser que ça pouvait être un moment hors des sentiers battus du système scolaire, une espèce d’échappée belle. Mais finalement, on est dans un trouble, et l’épaisseur un peu cryptée du trouble se diffuse dans le film.

Le film est très à l’écoute du ressenti des adolescents, qui sont en train de revendiquer leurs droits, d’exprimer une souffrance. Le fait qu’il sorte dans ce moment de manifestation, de lutte [ l’entretien a été réalisé avant la manifestation du 17 octobre, ndlr ], qu’est-ce que vous inspire ?

Quand on sent la porosité, l’écho, la caisse de résonance que peut être le cinéma, c’est très réjouissant. Tout à coup, il y a une espèce de prise de relais avec le réel, qui permet que les discussions autour du film puissent agir au présent.

Ce que ça m’évoque aussi, c’est que je trouve ça un signal extrêmement encourageant, satisfaisant, de se dire que, dans cette période préélectorale, plutôt que d’attendre l’avancée inexorable du pire à quoi on était condamné, la jeunesse prend la parole, bouge cette espèce de fixité de l’institution et des chances électorales, et démontre sa capacité de réflexion, d’organisation et d’action.

Dans le film, il y a l’évocation de Parcoursup, mais aussi celle des conditions d’un système éducatif qui n’est pas réformé depuis des décennies. Ça traduit non seulement un état de fait concret, matériel, mais aussi une appréhension d’un monde angoissant, et leur besoin, à un moment donné, de se situer et de prendre part. C’est ça aussi, l’initiation. C’est ce que Mercier dit à ses élèves : « Qu’est-ce que vous voyez, vous ? C’est vous qui allez être les créateurs de votre réflexion, de votre élaboration politique . »

Qu’est-ce que le tournage vous a appris sur la jeunesse d’aujourd’hui ?

Sur le tournage, ce qui m’a énormément impressionnée, c’est comment ils se sont emparés de la scène du débat politique avec autonomie. Toutes les luttes contemporaines qui, pour ma génération, ont été des déflagrations, ils les ont intégrées. Les questions de rapports de domination, de pouvoir, la question du genre, la fluidité : il y a quelque chose qui s’est intégré, incorporé, qui a été pris en main par cette nouvelle génération, avec des outils qui leur permettent d’agir, et pas juste de les manipuler comme des concepts. Donc plutôt que de se dire que cette jeunesse est juste abêtie devant des réseaux et ne sait pas discerner le vrai du faux avec les fake news , là, on voit qu’on a une jeunesse active et déterminée.

Vous avez 42 ans. Est-ce que le film vous a fait regarder dans le rétroviseur et repenser à l’ado que vous avez été à la fin des années 1990, ou début des années 2000 ?

Clairement. Et c’est génial, parce que ça m’a vraiment remise en contact avec l’incandescence de l’adolescence, cette sensation d’illimité, cette sensation d’avoir une puissance d’agir illimitée, d’avoir cette impudence et cette imprudence. Ça m’a énormément émue, parce que ce sont des sentiments, des impressions dont je me souviens très bien et qui sont vraiment un état émotionnel d’adolescence.

Et aussi comment le personnage de Toni est dans son désir pour James, qui n’arrive pas à exister comme il le souhaiterait. Ce rapport à l’énergie qu’on est prêt à décupler par rapport à des désirs secrets, des désirs cachés, l’inventivité dont on fait preuve, la capacité à différer son désir. Tout ça m’a vraiment remise avec des sensations que j’ai traversées adolescente. Et en même temps, maintenant, je ne suis pas mécontente de savoir qu’il y a une fin, qu’on meurt. [ rires ] Mais ce que je veux dire, c’est que c’était très étonnant, parce que je ne l’ai pas oubliée, cette période, elle existe. Mais là, c’était comme sentir une odeur et que ça réveille un souvenir.

En interview, Marine Atlan nous avait confié que fabriquer ce film l’avait fait renouer avec son histoire familiale, ses origines tunisiennes . Vous êtes d’origine corse. Est-ce que ça vous a procuré un effet similaire ?

C’est intéressant, cette question, parce que l’héritage, je trouve, dans le film, est vachement présent. C’est bien l’héritage collectif, des grandes œuvres qui ont fondé notre civilisation, qui fait qu’on a des signifiants et des référents communs. Et aussi l’héritage familial, et comment ces deux héritages ont la capacité de générer des révélations.

Je suis très touchée par le personnage de Toni, qui est comme chargé de quelque chose, d’une histoire qui ne lui appartient pas tout à fait, mais qui lui donne en même temps ce désir de le délirer, cet héritage, et de le transformer pour aspirer à autre chose. Et en même temps, il y a quelque chose de plus lourd qui agit sur lui malgré lui. Quand il découvre le récit de ses origines, c’est une grande perte de foi.

Moi, ça m’a fait un effet dans la mesure où, à l’adolescence, j’ai reconnecté avec une partie de mon histoire familiale. Mon arrière-grand-père [ Jean Nicoli, enseignant, membre de la SFIO puis du Parti communiste. Dénoncé, il a été fusillé en 1943 pour espionnage militaire, ndlr ] a été une figure tutélaire. Il a dirigé la résistance en Corse, a été torturé et tué par les fascistes italiens, et il est devenu un héros en Corse. Il a été pendant des années une figure d’autorité et une référence pour moi par rapport à des valeurs humanistes et, en même temps, son corps a été massacré, donc c’est une histoire de violence inouïe. Et je me rappelle qu’adolescente, et c’est aussi pour ça que je parle de Toni, on est pris dans cette histoire, mais c’est crypté. On ne discerne pas encore ce qu’on en fait et à quel endroit on trouve sa place.

article_text:
James Gunn took to Threads on Saturday to defend the DCU and his decision to expand the universe with “individual stories” amid criticism that his films aren’t building toward a major crossover event.

Responding to a commenter who pointed out that Gunn doesn’t necessarily need to lay the foundation for one totally interconnected universe, the DC Studios co-head wrote, “I couldn’t agree more.” “DCU is just an alternate universe; we can enter at any location or time and tell THAT story. I dislike the idea that individual stories aren’t meaningful unless they lead to something else. People not understanding this is strange to me, because ‘Star Wars’ has essentially been doing this for 50 years across movies, shows, games and books, admittedly without the tonal variety,” he wrote.

Related Stories

'The Pitt' And 'All Her Fault' Among the Winners of Inaugural Easterseals Disability Arts & Culture Awards

Gunn pointed out that this approach doesn’t mean there isn’t any connectivity, adding that the “Superman” saga begins with “Superman” and extends into “Man of Tomorrow,” “and contains many characters we’ve introduced in other stories.” “But that doesn’t mean those other stories only exist to set up what’s happening there. I would love people to be seeing ‘Clayface’ because it’s a great, fun horror movie unto itself, not because of where else Clayface will show up three movies from now,” he concluded.

Popular on Variety

In the post that Gunn responded to, the user had replied to an image that listed out his DC Universe foundation — “Superman,” “Peacemaker,” “Supergirl,” “Creature Commandos,” “Clayface” and “Lanters” — followed by the text: “What is this building towards???”

“Clayface,” which his theaters on Friday, is Gunn’s latest DCU installment, following 2025’s “Superman” and this year’s “Supergirl.” (Ahead of the film’s release, comic fans pointed out that the character, who has never been the subject of a standalone feature film, is a considerably nicher choice than previous DCU films.) It generated $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, comfortably taking the No. 1 spot at the box office.

Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star also known as Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan also star.

Variety’s Guy Lodge called the film “its own ugly animal; perhaps the characters and conflicts introduced here would pall if given the franchise treatment, but in the context of a single, genre-melding romp, they’re fresh and ickily enjoyable.”

Gunn’s next film, “ Superman: Man of Tomorrow ,” hits theaters July 9, 2027.

article_text:
As artificial intelligence continues to advance, animators are increasingly facing questions about the future of their craft and the role of human creativity in filmmaking. But the majority are not interested in letting AI into their art of storytelling.

At Variety ‘s “Pixels and Pencils” panel in Savannah, Georgia, on Monday, leading filmmakers discussed the process of bringing animated stories to life and why technology can’t replace the work behind them. Six panelists joined Variety ‘s Clayton Davis for the discussion, which was moderated in partnership with SCAD Savannah Film Festival. They included Brad Bird for Netflix’s “Ray Gunn”; Daniel Chong for Pixar’s “Hoppers”; Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado for DreamWorks Animation’s “Forgotten Island”; Travis Knight for Laika’s “Wildwood”; and Leah Nelson for Independent Film Company’s “Tangles.”

Related Stories

Jason Sudeikis Hopes to Continue ‘Ted Lasso’ for Season 5, Says Coverage of Split From Olivia Wilde Missed a ‘Million Little Things’: ‘It’s Always More Complicated’

Meg Weichman, the artistic manager of SCAD’s Theatres and Festivals, introduced this year’s panel, which she described as a celebration of the “imagination, artistry and collaboration that brings extraordinary animated stories to life.”

But to make something “extraordinary” requires significant effort, which is part of what makes the process “magical,” Chong said.

“Every set, every character, every piece of cloth, every piece of hair, every moment of atmosphere, all of that is created and made from ground zero. There’s no camera you can point at,” Chong told the audience. “It’s just completely fabricated and made and created, and that’s a pretty amazing thing, because that’s one of the reasons why I think these movies take so long, is because they have to create their own world.”

Creating an animated film typically takes well over a year — and sometimes much, more more. From the first idea to its big-screen release, Bird’s “Ray Gunn” took roughly 30 years to finalize, though he wasn’t consistently working on the film throughout that period.

But Bird was willing to put in the work, saying that a good story “has to come from life. You can’t create the illusion of life without having one, and that’s what we are in charge of — making the illusion of life and bringing people to something new.”

“Wildwood” also required an extensive production process, especially considering it used stop-motion animation. The film used 2,800 shots, a process Knight described as a “pain.”

“Stop motion is progressive. You start on frame one and you work your way all the way through in slow motion until you have a performance,” he said. “There is something extraordinarily magical about being a part of that.”

Despite the time and effort needed, the filmmakers said the process is what makes work meaningful. Chong added, “When you see people taunting that, ‘Oh, I can make this with the click of a button,’ or, ‘I can do this with these shortcuts,’ I think we just have to have faith that these processes are the way they are, and they’re as hard as they are to make for a reason, because that’s what makes these movies great and that’s what makes them resonate with humans.”

The panelists agreed that the humanity behind these films allows stories to resonate with audiences — something AI can’t replicate. But the industry’s future remains uncertain as technology advances and animators continue to adapt. Bird advised artists in the audience to keep learning the ins and outs of animation as the field evolves .

The filmmakers also discussed how different animation styles can shape of story. Deciding whether to use 2D animation, 3D animation, stop motion or even claymation depends on the film’s narrative, Mercado said.

“It really is the story that dictates the visual storytelling and drive of the characters,” he shared. “That’s how we were able to play with various styles of anime and manga that followed the character point of view in these sections of [‘Forgotten Island’].”

Crawford added, “For ‘Forgotten Island,’ we’re like, ‘This is an exploration of memories and how we experience them’ and thinking we all reflect memories in different ways. To have the animation style switch up depending on who the teller of the memory is was just a really exciting opportunity.”

The panelists also challenged the common misconceptions of working as an animator, which for “Tangles” director Nelson, included actually needing to be an animator.

“What I had to do, because I’m not an animator, was do everything else to communicate the vision — anything I could think of to communicate to my team what I hoped for and what I wanted to fight for,” she said. “I used all the other tools I could think of. I did a lot of acting references. I filmed myself doing the actions if I couldn’t draw it.”

article_text:
La natura morta può ancora essere un campo di ricerca? In Hei-ho , Marta Ravasi torna a confrontarsi con uno dei soggetti più sedimentati della storia della pittura per portarlo verso una dimensione sempre più prossima all’astrazione. Frutti, ciotole e composizioni essenziali diventano così il punto di partenza per una ricerca sulla materia, sul colore e sulla percezione.

Visitabile alla Galleria Acappella di Napoli fino al 9 novembre 2026, la mostra è il terzo appuntamento del percorso dell’artista con la galleria, iniziato nel 2023 con Bucce . In questa occasione, Ravasi, nata a Merate nel 1987 e oggi attiva a Milano, presenta un ciclo di oli su tela di piccolo formato in cui la riconoscibilità del soggetto rimane il punto di partenza, mentre la pittura progressivamente se ne allontana.

Marta Ravasi, un paradosso pittorico in mostra

Il soggetto è invariato: frutta sferica, composizioni elementari, formati piccoli. I titoli delle opere in mostra ( Pesche , Frutti , Cinque Frutti , Ciotola ) confermano la scelta di un vocabolario volutamente neutro. È proprio dentro questo perimetro ristretto che Ravasi costruisce la propria varietà formale.

Le dimensioni restano contenute, tra i 20 × 25 cm e un massimo di 37 × 46 cm. Le superfici si affinano o si ispessiscono in aree precise della tela, le composizioni trovano nuove geometrie, la scelta cromatica si arricchisce pur rimanendo entro una gamma definita: rosa, arancioni, bruni, tonalità carnali che sottraggono i frutti alla loro evidenza botanica e li avvicinano a qualcosa di corporeo.

Anche il pennello procede in direzioni diverse: tratti frenetici in alcune zone, più composti e controllati in altre, mentre il focus è generalmente decentrato. Lo sguardo non trova un punto di approdo fisso, ma attraversa la superficie come un campo aperto.

Il risultato è una pittura che oscilla con coerenza tra riconoscibilità e astrazione. L’ispirazione novecentesca è evidente, in particolare nella tradizione di chi ha guardato alla natura morta non come a un genere minore ma come a un laboratorio formale: da Morandi alla pittura analitica, fino a quelle ricerche europee che hanno fatto del quotidiano un pretesto per interrogare la struttura stessa dell’immagine.

La frutta viene così svuotata della propria evidenza e ricostruita attraverso volumi atmosferici, spazi pieni e vuoti che assumono configurazioni differenti da una tela all’altra. Il dato riconoscibile rimane ma sembra progressivamente perdere la propria funzione descrittiva.

Hei-ho: fermarsi a guardare

Hei-ho è un’interiezione onomatopeica, un richiamo, una sorta di sveglia. Il titolo sembra rievocare la cantilena infantile di Biancaneve e i sette nani ma qui diventa soprattutto un invito a spostare l’attenzione verso una visione meno razionale della quotidianità.

Nel testo critico di Elizabeth Germana Arthur questa intuizione viene sviluppata attraverso riferimenti mitologici e filosofici: il Diòs enkèfalos degli antichi, il cibo così squisito da meritare la prossimità con la testa di Zeus, diventa una chiave per leggere la tensione implicita nella forma sferica. Una forma apparentemente stabile ma capace di sfuggire a se stessa con una lieve pressione, di diventare ovale, gonfiarsi, piegarsi. Il cerchio come forma che più di tutte sembra poter eccedere i propri confini.

In questa dimensione, ogni frutto dipinto da Ravasi è materia compiuta e promessa di compimento insieme, mentre la pittura diventa il luogo di un’ulteriore gestazione. Il percorso di Ravasi, sempre più orientato verso una dimensione prossima all’astrazione e sempre più raffinato nella gestione della materia, trova in questa terza collaborazione con Acappella una nuova tappa di consolidamento.

article_text:
"Angefangen hat's erst in Berlin", sagte Lovis Corinth über seine Karriere. Was die Hauptstadt mit seiner Malerei machte, zeigt nun eine große Ausstellung in der Berlinischen Galerie. Wir verlosen Tickets

Lovis Corinth war 43 Jahre alt, als er 1901 München verließ und nach Berlin zog. Eine Entscheidung, die er nicht bereuen sollte. "München war nicht der richtige Ort für mich. Angefangen hat's erst in Berlin", befand er später. In der Hauptstadt wurde er zum gefragten Porträtisten, mischte in der Berliner Secession mit und fand zu einer Malerei, die immer freier, farbiger und expressiver wurde.

Corinth hatte eine Vorliebe für große Auftritte. Er malte sich selbst als Bacchus, Ritter oder Derwisch, porträtierte die Schauspielerin Tilla Durieux und entwarf Kostüme und Bühnenbilder für den Regisseur Max Reinhardt. Auch seine eigene Wohnung und Familie lieferten einiges an Bildmaterial. Seine Frau Charlotte Berend-Corinth etwa, selbst Malerin und einst seine Schülerin, taucht immer wieder in seinen Werken auf. Daneben entstanden Stillleben, deren Blumen und Früchte unter den schnellen, pastosen Pinselstrichen beinahe ihre Form verlieren.

Wie sehr Berlin Corinths Kunst veränderte, untersucht nun die Berlinische Galerie in der Ausstellung "Lovis Corinth. Dann kam Berlin!". Zu sehen sind rund 80 seiner Werke sowie 30 Arbeiten von Zeitgenossen und ehemaligen Schülerinnen und Schülern, darunter August Macke und Minna Beckmann-Tube. Die Schau erzählt damit auch von der Kunstszene um 1900, in der private Malschulen gerade für Frauen wichtige Ausbildungsorte waren. Corinths Erfolgsgeschichte bekam nach seinem Tod 1925 allerdings einen bitteren Nachtrag: Die Nationalsozialisten beschlagnahmten später mehr als 350 seiner Werke aus deutschen Museen, vor allem aus seiner expressiven Spätphase.

Monopol verlost 5 × 2 Tickets für die Ausstellung "Lovis Corinth. Dann kam Berlin!", die noch bis zum 25. Januar 2027 in der Berlinischen Galerie zu sehen ist. Für die Teilnahme schicken Sie eine E-Mail mit Ihrem Vor- und Nachnamen und dem Betreff "Lovis Corinth" bis Donnerstag, 12. November, 14 Uhr, an info@monopol-magazin.de . Die Gewinnerinnen und Gewinner werden per E-Mail benachrichtigt. Der Rechtsweg ist ausgeschlossen.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Flawless , the British-American company that spent $100 million building SAG-AFTRA-endorsed AI dubbing technology used on movies like Fall , has sold its intellectual property.

In an unusual deal that raises questions about Flawless’ future, TBellScout, a startup owned by Dutch tech billionaire Steven Schuurman, has acquired the company’s TrueSync dubbing technology and DeepEditor, an AI post-production tool.

Schuurman, who founded Dutch software company Elastic, confirmed the acquisition to Deadline. He declined to comment further. Flawless’ co-founder Scott Mann declined to comment.

Related Stories

'The Office' Editor Thinks AI Can Make Comedy Funnier

'Fall' Sequel Cast & Plot Details Revealed With 'Outlander', 'Bridgerton' & 'Grantchester' Stars In The Lead Roles -- TIFF Market

Deadline understands that Flawless’ technology was held by Flawless Holdings Limited, its UK trading company founded in 2020.

Watch on Deadline

Earlier this month, Flawless Holdings Limited filed for administration, which is similar to Chapter 11 bankruptcy. But unlike in the U.S., where directors remain in control of the business, insolvency specialist BTG took over the company’s operations and sold the tech to TBellScout.

Sprk Capital, a UK-based tech lender, appointed BTG as Flawless’ administrator. Sprk Capital holds fixed and floating charges over Flawless, forms of finance repayment security granted to a lender.

The circumstances of the IP sale are unclear at this point, but it follows Amit Kapur becoming Flawless’ co-CEO in March after serving as a board member since 2024. Kapur did not respond to a request for comment.

Mann and co-founder Nick Lynes remain in control of Flawless AI Inc., the U.S. business through which the duo cultivated relationships and deals with Hollywood studios by taking a consent-based approach to AI. Mann and Lynes are said to be exploring a new venture, however.

Flawless raised the $100M through wealthy individuals, rather than venture capital. Its technology platform and filmmaking tools consisted of three main aspects: visual dubbing tool TrueSync, which was named one of Time Magazine’s Best Inventions; DeepEditor, a tool that allows for dialogue and performance changes without costly reshoots, synchronizing actors’ mouths to new lines; and the rights management platform Artistic Rights Treasury.

Flawless’ technology has been used on hundreds of Hollywood productions, though much of its work has been under the radar because studios have declined to disclose their use of artificial intelligence.

Flawless’ tools were used on Swedish sci-fi hit Watch the Skies , making it the first theatrical full-length feature to use immersive AI dubbing. Flawless partnered with XYZ Films to release the English-language version of the film in U.S. theaters.

Other translation projects include Michel Gondry’s The Book of Solutions , Judo thriller Tatami , South Korean title Smugglers , Stéphan Castang’s Vincent Must Die , and Berlin Film Festival opener The Light .

Mann doubles as a filmmaker, directing movies including Fall , the 2022 thriller about two friends who get stuck up a 2,000-foot radio tower in the desert. Fall became a case study for Flawless’ technology, using AI to visually dub swearing out of the movie to secure a PG-13 rating.

title_original: Best Actress Frontrunner Julianne Moore Nailed ‘The Debut’ by Singing, Styling Her Hair Like Liza Minnelli, and Avoiding Playing ‘Some Suffering Mom’
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Hello, I’m Julie,” said a radiant Julianne Moore, holding out her hand as she popped out of the elevator at Middleburg, Virginia’s Salamander Resort. Her hair was red, her skin was white, her dress as yellow as gold. A few hours later after a rapturous Middleburg Film Festival reaction to “The Debut” (December 11), we talked in a hotel meeting room. The A24 crowdpleaser has been wowing audiences and critics since Telluride.", "links": [{"text": "“The Debut”", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/the-debut-review-jesse-eisenberg-julianne-moore-1235215173/"}, {"text": "wowing audiences", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/industry/virginia-film-festival-opens-the-debut-1235223353/"}, {"text": "critics", "url": "https://www.metacritic.com/movie/the-debut-2026/"}, {"text": "Telluride.", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/awards/predictions/telluride-oscar-analysis-john-malkovich-a24-elizabeth-holmes-doc-1235215558/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Jesse Eisenberg has done it again. His follow-up to “A Real Pain,” which won Kieran Culkin the Supporting Actor Oscar, could score Best Actress for Moore . The musical comedy has earned Moore raves on the festival circuit for her role as a sad suburban homemaker turned anxious aspiring actress in a New Jersey community theater. A sixth Oscar nomination is inevitable, and possibly a second Oscar win after “Still Alice” in 2015. It’s hard to believe she launched her career in 1988 as a regular on soap opera “As the World Turns.”", "links": [{"text": "Jesse Eisenberg", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/interviews/jesse-eisenberg-the-debut-interview-1235215210/"}, {"text": "Moore", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/julianne-moore/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/GettyImages-2191837091-e1794246315407.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Kelly O'Sullivan, Alex Thompson at the 2025 Spirit Awards Nominees Brunch at Hotel Casa del Mar on January 4, 2025 in Santa Monica, California. (Photo by JC Olivera/Variety via Getty Images)", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/MixCollage-06-Nov-2026-03-02-PM-8955.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "'La Bola Negra' directors Los Javis and 'Project Hail Mary' directors Lord and Miller.", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Moore is the current Best Actress frontrunner, even though she has won before. Sometimes nabbing an Oscar is a disadvantage in the Oscar race. But not if the performance is undeniable: Katharine Hepburn holds the record with four, while nipping at her heels are three-time winners Meryl Streep, Frances McDormand, Jack Nicholson, and Sean Penn."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eisenberg wrote a rich character for Moore, knowing what the veteran actress could do with the childlike housewife Mona who, in order to learn how to act, must find herself. The director and actress had worked together on “When You Finish Saving the World” (2022). “[‘ The Debut ‘] is about this woman who has been chewed up but not spit out,” said Eisenberg, quoting Mona’s signature song. “It’s my point of view through somebody I consider a muse. I was writing something about myself as a seven-year-old in 1990, but I couldn’t picture anybody else except her doing it.”", "links": [{"text": "The Debut", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/the-debut/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/jxm6hqpj3premieres_WhenYouFinishSavingtheWorld_Still1.jpeg?w=650", "alt": "94180007.JPG", "caption": "“When You Finish Saving the World” Beth Garrabrant", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It helped that Moore had told Eisenberg exactly what she was looking for. “I said I had just done ‘Dear Evan Hansen,’ and I loved singing, and I would love to have another opportunity,” she said. “I told him that I would love to do more comedy, and I didn’t want to play some suffering mom.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eisenberg put all of this in the screenplay, “but in the most surprising and inventive way,” she said. “He’s such a specific writer. He’s so incredibly empathetic. He has a compassionate worldview. He understands creativity. All of that stuff went into this wonderful and delightful story. It’s joyful and life-affirming too.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Moore didn’t know she was playing a seven-year-old version of Eisenberg until he started telling that to the press. “Then he was like, ‘This is my experience of being a kid and going to community theater.’ But I could sense that there was a personal point of view in it. I very much felt with Mona that she was on a subjective journey, and that he was inside of that. With Mona, I always knew he was looking through her.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The Debut” is told from her point of view, as she tries to talk the overbearing local community theater director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) into hiring her, an untrained actress. He does it because he has no one else. But first, he must teach her how to act."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/TheDebut_Still02R.jpg?w=650", "alt": "'The Debut'", "caption": "Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore in “The Debut” Courtesy of A24", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mona dresses like a schoolgirl, with skirts, blouses, cardigan sweaters. “She’s so contained, and the way she learns is so literal,” said Moore, “the way a baby learns, like, you make a face at a baby, the baby makes a face back, but they don’t have intention behind it. But they’re learning things in an exterior way, and then they match it with feeling later on. So everything she’s doing is a childlike way of learning.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mona goes from an invisible nonentity in her own home to someone who demands attention. “She’s a kid who has found friends for the first time,” said Eisenberg. “She’s the girl who transferred to the right school at seven years old, and then the first rehearsal happens, and she is told she is terrible, and she has no idea why. And it’s the girl who transferred to the right school and gets an F on the very first test, and then the rest of the semester is panicking, and all she’s seeing is everybody else get A’s, and she still has the F, and she doesn’t know what to do. And then the teacher pulls her aside and says, ‘You either show up, or you are out on your ass.’ And something switches in her, and she makes the decision: ‘I am going to show up.’ And she begins to turn into a monster.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The theater troupe embraces Mona as she unfolds like a flower. “We’ve been like those theater kids cracking corny jokes and finding community,” said Moore. “It’s all done with so much affection. Jesse looks at that world with not a hint of malice.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Giamatti’s director relentlessly pushes the newbie through her paces until they have a powerful confrontation on the empty stage where he forces her to break down. Eisenberg reduced the actors’ anxiety by placing the eight-page showstopper in the middle of the shoot: not the beginning, and not the end. On the first day he went over to Moore’s apartment to talk about the movie. He said, “I really don’t want you to worry about that scene. I don’t want you to worry about memorizing that because I know that as an actor, I would I lose my mind. I would just be drilling it all the time, and I wouldn’t be able to concentrate. We’re going to have a teleprompter on that day. So don’t worry about it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So Moore worked on it normally, she said, “like I worked on everything else in the movie. So when we got to it, I knew it. I didn’t need a teleprompter. He knew instinctively as a director and an actor that what scares us sometimes is just a volume of language. He didn’t want to freeze me up. And having a partner like Paul who was so awake and aware and generous made it a pleasure. We were enjoying it when we did shoot it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Moore and Giamatti had never worked together before. She once introduced herself to him in a bookstore in Montauk. “He was very shy,” she said. “He is the greatest scene partner. I didn’t expect him to be so generous. He’s so funny, and he’s so dear. He’s present, incredibly modest, and as a partner, so available. Paul and I would work on it occasionally. When we were doing that scene, the rhythm was so important in it. You throw something, he hits it right back. It was our sense together of keeping it aloft, keeping it moving, keeping the river flowing. It felt electric with the two of us.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The big blowout happens early in the story. “In a lot of movies, that kind of set piece would happen later,” said Moore. “Instead, it’s like a discovery place. It’s where she starts to begin to unlock herself emotionally, but she doesn’t learn from it. She comes in the next day, and starts to rehearse. And her belief is that acting is size, that it’s just huge, right? That’s when she starts yelling. She thinks it’s about being loud, which then allows her to go on the next journey with Jerry, where he says, ‘Let’s talk about feeling and reality and intention.’ So she’s slowly putting these pieces together. But that’s the first moment where she attaches something outside of herself to her own emotion.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The whole shoot was fast, as Eisenberg didn’t have time to muck about and often shot just one take of a scene. “She and Paul Giamatti are so good on take one,” said Eisenberg. “It’s embarrassing. This is a small budget movie. The first two days of our schedule, we filmed in one day. The first two days, which were big ensemble musical numbers, we filmed in one day because we were prepared as a crew, but the actors were perfect on take one.”", "links": [{"text": "Paul Giamatti", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/paul-giamatti/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/4526.webp?w=650", "alt": "The Debut", "caption": "‘The Debut’ A24", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Moore didn’t feel rushed. “It doesn’t feel, working with Jesse, like you’re moving too fast,” she said. “Working in independent film, you’re always moving quickly because you need to. You don’t have the time. You don’t have the money. So you want to move through things quickly. But I never felt rushed with him. I never I never felt like I was leaving something, that I didn’t get to complete something.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The challenge for Moore, as it is for every actor shooting out of order, was making her character changes seamless. Eisenberg started with the theater scenes, then shot her family, and then jumped into Mona’s increasing weirdness. “The hardest thing always is making sure that you’ve pitched things correctly,” Moore said. “You want to make sure that you’ve managed to match it to another scene. So it was always hard to figure out. That’s our job.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eisenberg wanted Mona to move from looking quite childlike in the beginning, and swiftly move through her evolving transformations. Moore had fun with the costumes, figuring out the crazy wigs, makeup, and outfits in the second half. “Jesse had written that Mona electrocutes herself and destroys her hair, and that she was going to get her hair cut,” said Moore, “but he hadn’t written in a color change. article_text:
“Hello, I’m Julie,” said a radiant Julianne Moore, holding out her hand as she popped out of the elevator at Middleburg, Virginia’s Salamander Resort. Her hair was red, her skin was white, her dress as yellow as gold. A few hours later after a rapturous Middleburg Film Festival reaction to “The Debut” (December 11), we talked in a hotel meeting room. The A24 crowdpleaser has been wowing audiences and critics since Telluride.

Jesse Eisenberg has done it again. His follow-up to “A Real Pain,” which won Kieran Culkin the Supporting Actor Oscar, could score Best Actress for Moore . The musical comedy has earned Moore raves on the festival circuit for her role as a sad suburban homemaker turned anxious aspiring actress in a New Jersey community theater. A sixth Oscar nomination is inevitable, and possibly a second Oscar win after “Still Alice” in 2015. It’s hard to believe she launched her career in 1988 as a regular on soap opera “As the World Turns.”

Moore is the current Best Actress frontrunner, even though she has won before. Sometimes nabbing an Oscar is a disadvantage in the Oscar race. But not if the performance is undeniable: Katharine Hepburn holds the record with four, while nipping at her heels are three-time winners Meryl Streep, Frances McDormand, Jack Nicholson, and Sean Penn.

Eisenberg wrote a rich character for Moore, knowing what the veteran actress could do with the childlike housewife Mona who, in order to learn how to act, must find herself. The director and actress had worked together on “When You Finish Saving the World” (2022). “[‘ The Debut ‘] is about this woman who has been chewed up but not spit out,” said Eisenberg, quoting Mona’s signature song. “It’s my point of view through somebody I consider a muse. I was writing something about myself as a seven-year-old in 1990, but I couldn’t picture anybody else except her doing it.”

It helped that Moore had told Eisenberg exactly what she was looking for. “I said I had just done ‘Dear Evan Hansen,’ and I loved singing, and I would love to have another opportunity,” she said. “I told him that I would love to do more comedy, and I didn’t want to play some suffering mom.”

Eisenberg put all of this in the screenplay, “but in the most surprising and inventive way,” she said. “He’s such a specific writer. He’s so incredibly empathetic. He has a compassionate worldview. He understands creativity. All of that stuff went into this wonderful and delightful story. It’s joyful and life-affirming too.”

Moore didn’t know she was playing a seven-year-old version of Eisenberg until he started telling that to the press. “Then he was like, ‘This is my experience of being a kid and going to community theater.’ But I could sense that there was a personal point of view in it. I very much felt with Mona that she was on a subjective journey, and that he was inside of that. With Mona, I always knew he was looking through her.”

“The Debut” is told from her point of view, as she tries to talk the overbearing local community theater director Jerry (Paul Giamatti) into hiring her, an untrained actress. He does it because he has no one else. But first, he must teach her how to act.

Mona dresses like a schoolgirl, with skirts, blouses, cardigan sweaters. “She’s so contained, and the way she learns is so literal,” said Moore, “the way a baby learns, like, you make a face at a baby, the baby makes a face back, but they don’t have intention behind it. But they’re learning things in an exterior way, and then they match it with feeling later on. So everything she’s doing is a childlike way of learning.”

Mona goes from an invisible nonentity in her own home to someone who demands attention. “She’s a kid who has found friends for the first time,” said Eisenberg. “She’s the girl who transferred to the right school at seven years old, and then the first rehearsal happens, and she is told she is terrible, and she has no idea why. And it’s the girl who transferred to the right school and gets an F on the very first test, and then the rest of the semester is panicking, and all she’s seeing is everybody else get A’s, and she still has the F, and she doesn’t know what to do. And then the teacher pulls her aside and says, ‘You either show up, or you are out on your ass.’ And something switches in her, and she makes the decision: ‘I am going to show up.’ And she begins to turn into a monster.”

The theater troupe embraces Mona as she unfolds like a flower. “We’ve been like those theater kids cracking corny jokes and finding community,” said Moore. “It’s all done with so much affection. Jesse looks at that world with not a hint of malice.”

Giamatti’s director relentlessly pushes the newbie through her paces until they have a powerful confrontation on the empty stage where he forces her to break down. Eisenberg reduced the actors’ anxiety by placing the eight-page showstopper in the middle of the shoot: not the beginning, and not the end. On the first day he went over to Moore’s apartment to talk about the movie. He said, “I really don’t want you to worry about that scene. I don’t want you to worry about memorizing that because I know that as an actor, I would I lose my mind. I would just be drilling it all the time, and I wouldn’t be able to concentrate. We’re going to have a teleprompter on that day. So don’t worry about it.”

So Moore worked on it normally, she said, “like I worked on everything else in the movie. So when we got to it, I knew it. I didn’t need a teleprompter. He knew instinctively as a director and an actor that what scares us sometimes is just a volume of language. He didn’t want to freeze me up. And having a partner like Paul who was so awake and aware and generous made it a pleasure. We were enjoying it when we did shoot it.”

Moore and Giamatti had never worked together before. She once introduced herself to him in a bookstore in Montauk. “He was very shy,” she said. “He is the greatest scene partner. I didn’t expect him to be so generous. He’s so funny, and he’s so dear. He’s present, incredibly modest, and as a partner, so available. Paul and I would work on it occasionally. When we were doing that scene, the rhythm was so important in it. You throw something, he hits it right back. It was our sense together of keeping it aloft, keeping it moving, keeping the river flowing. It felt electric with the two of us.”

The big blowout happens early in the story. “In a lot of movies, that kind of set piece would happen later,” said Moore. “Instead, it’s like a discovery place. It’s where she starts to begin to unlock herself emotionally, but she doesn’t learn from it. She comes in the next day, and starts to rehearse. And her belief is that acting is size, that it’s just huge, right? That’s when she starts yelling. She thinks it’s about being loud, which then allows her to go on the next journey with Jerry, where he says, ‘Let’s talk about feeling and reality and intention.’ So she’s slowly putting these pieces together. But that’s the first moment where she attaches something outside of herself to her own emotion.”

The whole shoot was fast, as Eisenberg didn’t have time to muck about and often shot just one take of a scene. “She and Paul Giamatti are so good on take one,” said Eisenberg. “It’s embarrassing. This is a small budget movie. The first two days of our schedule, we filmed in one day. The first two days, which were big ensemble musical numbers, we filmed in one day because we were prepared as a crew, but the actors were perfect on take one.”

Moore didn’t feel rushed. “It doesn’t feel, working with Jesse, like you’re moving too fast,” she said. “Working in independent film, you’re always moving quickly because you need to. You don’t have the time. You don’t have the money. So you want to move through things quickly. But I never felt rushed with him. I never I never felt like I was leaving something, that I didn’t get to complete something.”

The challenge for Moore, as it is for every actor shooting out of order, was making her character changes seamless. Eisenberg started with the theater scenes, then shot her family, and then jumped into Mona’s increasing weirdness. “The hardest thing always is making sure that you’ve pitched things correctly,” Moore said. “You want to make sure that you’ve managed to match it to another scene. So it was always hard to figure out. That’s our job.”

Eisenberg wanted Mona to move from looking quite childlike in the beginning, and swiftly move through her evolving transformations. Moore had fun with the costumes, figuring out the crazy wigs, makeup, and outfits in the second half. “Jesse had written that Mona electrocutes herself and destroys her hair, and that she was going to get her hair cut,” said Moore, “but he hadn’t written in a color change. We were messing around with it and trying to figure out what to do with hair and makeup and wardrobe and we had this idea that by having her dye her hair dark and chop it off, I wanted to homage the great ladies of musical theater, Liza Minnelli and Chita Rivera and Patti LuPone. It’s a wonderful Easter egg for that character.”

Making everything easier for Moore was actor-turned-director Eisenberg, who’d tell her when to ‘raise the stakes’ or ‘go hotter.’ “He’s maybe the most collaborative person I’ve ever worked with my entire life,” said Moore. “He listens to everyone. He asks people for opinions. He’ll ask people for notes, in a way that I would be like, ‘you don’t have to do that. This is your movie. It’s your creation.’ But he does collate opinion in a way. He’s fascinating in his generosity.”

Needless to say, singing her centerpiece song (“This City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Hasn’t Spit Me Out”) was nervous-making, given that Moore was surrounded by Broadway super-belters like Tony winners Danny Burstein and Bonnie Tillman. “These people have the voices of angels,” said Moore. “When I did sing that song for the first time, and they’re all sitting there watching me, I think they did feel worried for me because they have so much ease. The song that she sings is so beautiful. In the singing of the song, she’s attaching her own emotional experience suddenly to the song. She understands the song in the moment she’s singing that. Somehow she wants more, and she knows that this is an avenue for her to find that. And so it’s a journey back to herself: finding that creativity and connection and community brings her to an essential sense of self.”

If degree of difficulty counts with Oscar voters, Moore may have that advantage.
excerpt_original: The Oscar winner asked Jesse Eisenberg to write her a role that allowed her to do comedy. It could lead to her second statue.

article_text:
Internationally renowned art and photography book publisher Damiani Books has announced the launch of the Andrea Albertini Award , a new annual international prize honouring the legacy of its visionary founder and celebrating excellence in photography and art publishing.

Established to mark the twentieth anniversary of the publisher’s first books, the award invites readers worldwide to help select the most relevant Damiani book published in 2025.

The 14 Damiani books published in 2025 are in contention for the first Andrea Albertini Award.

Photography enthusiasts, collectors, artists and readers around the world are invited to vote for their three favourite Damiani books published in 2025, helping to determine the inaugural winner, which will be announced by 31 January 2027.

Founded in Bologna, Damiani has spent two decades bringing internationally acclaimed photographers and emerging talents to audiences worldwide, establishing the photobook as an artistic medium in its own right.

A LEGACY BUILT THROUGH PHOTOGRAPHY

Andrea Albertini, owner of a state-of-the-art printing house based in Bologna (Italy), founded Damiani Books with a belief in the power of photography and the importance of the printed book as a lasting expression of an artist’s vision.

From Bologna, he helped build an internationally recognised publishing house, creating a platform for established and emerging photographers whose work crosses the boundaries of art, fashion, documentary photography and contemporary culture.

The award celebrates his commitment to artistic excellence, creative collaboration and the enduring cultural significance of photography books.

Silvia Pesci, co-founder and Chairman of Damiani Books, said: “I am very proud of this award, which celebrates the memory of my beloved husband and his vision. Every book Damiani publishes deserves to win, but I am delighted to let our community of readers choose our photography book of the year.”

The prize also reflects a defining principle of independent publishing: that a book’s importance cannot be measured by commercial success alone, but also by the connection it establishes with its readers.

THE READERS HAVE THEIR SAY

Unlike conventional photography awards decided by a panel of expert judges, the Andrea Albertini Award has no jury: the prize is placed entirely in the hands of readers. All art books published by Damiani in the preceding year qualify automatically; magazines and calendars are excluded.

100% – Decided by readers

Half of the ranking comes from the books readers buy, measured by international sales in each title’s first twelve months; half from the books they vote for.

An Award Committee appointed by Damiani manages the process and confirms the final result according to the published rules. In the event of a tie, the award may be granted ex aequo. The winner will receive an award inspired by the gold record: their book framed alongside a commemorative plaque.

VOTE FOR THE FIRST ANDREA ALBERTINI AWARD

VOTING OPENS VOTING CLOSES WINNER ANNOUNCED Mon 2 November Fri 27 November By 31 January 2027

Voting opens on Monday 2 November and runs until Friday 27 November 2026. Readers select their three favourite titles from the 14 books in contention; each selected title receives one point. "茶の湯デザインの3000年史――中世日本では、大陸との交流のなかで喫茶の風習がもたらされ、やがて「茶の湯」として独自の伝統文化を形成していきます。喫茶に用いられ、そして喫茶の場を彩る道具には「唐物」とよばれる大陸の文物が珍重され、当時の人々の価値観や美意識による選別を経て、いわゆる「名物」として評価されるものも登場しました。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展ではこうした「唐物」が誕生する過程に焦点が当てられます。はるか中国古代にまでさかのぼって紹介され、胡銅（古銅）とよばれる花入を切り口として、金工品や陶磁器、漆工など、素材を越えた共通性にも着目しながら、茶の湯デザインを東アジア文化史のなかに再定位することが試みられます。さらに、これまで未解明であった胡銅の鋳造技術にせまる特集コーナーも設け、最新の研究成果もあわせて紹介されます。"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "唐物とは"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "古代・中世において中国などから輸入された諸物貨に冠せられた和訓の総称（『国史大辞典』）。なかでも日中貿易が盛んになった鎌倉～室町時代には、さまざまな種類の「唐物」がもたらされ、それらはやがて成立してくる茶の湯のなかで貴重な茶道具として珍重されるようになりました。ただし、当時「唐物」と認識されていた文物はかならずしも中国産にはかぎられず、朝鮮半島や東南アジアで制作されたものや、あるいは国産品も含まれます。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展では中世後期の日本で珍重された舶来の茶道具類を広く「唐物」とよび、中国文物を範としつつ、模倣やアレンジを加えて裾野が広がっていく茶の湯デザインの文化史的背景を、約三千年前の中国古代にまでさかのぼって紹介することが試みられます。"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "展覧会構成"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "I いにしえへのあこがれ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "いまから約三千年前、殷周時代に盛んにつくられた青銅器は、その造形レベルの高さからのちの時代の美術工芸の模範とされましたが、それだけでなく、周の時代は儒教のなかで理想の治世がなされた時代とされ、その遺風を伝える青銅器は特別に尊ばれるようになりました。「東洋のルネサンス」とも称される宋代では、こうした青銅器に対する関心が急速に高まり、同時代の陶磁器や金工品などのデザインにも強く影響をおよぼすようになります。本章では住友コレクションのほこる中国古代青銅器と、いにしえへのあこがれから生み出された工芸品をともに展示し、のちの「唐物」へと受け継がれるデザインの源流が紹介されます。"}, 規範の形成 宋元時代の喫茶文化と文物"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "宋代以降、士大夫と呼ばれる知識人層が当時の政治・文化の中心をになうようになり、彼らの価値観が強く反映された文物が重視されるようになります。同時に、点茶法とよばれる喫茶も流行し、その用途にかなう道具や、喫茶の空間を飾る工芸品も生み出されました。やがて、こうした文物にあらわされたデザインは、のちの時代まで受け継がれる「規範」を形成し、東アジアの文化に多大な影響を与えるようになります。本章では中国宋元時代の絵画・工芸作品を一堂に会し、この時代の中国で生み出された「古典」とはいかなるものかを探っていきます。"}, "text": "III 日中交易と喫茶文化の伝来"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "日本中世では、海上交易を通じて大陸との交流が活発におこなわれ、当時の最先端の流行であった喫茶文化にかかわる文物ももたらされることとなりました。それらが日本国内で特に珍重されるようになり、やがて「唐物」として茶の湯の形成に大きな役割を果たします。一方で、単に中国文化に追随するだけでなく、国内でそれを模したもの、そこから日本独自のデザインへと進化したものも生み出されています。本章では日本と大陸の交流の証、そしてメイドインジャパンの胎動を示す作品から、喫茶の受容と文化交流のあり方にせまっていきます。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/8-17.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "芦屋霰地真形釜　日本・室町／15世紀　芦屋釜の里", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/9-17.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "重要文化財　無爾可宣墨蹟　中国・南宋／咸淳4年（1268） 今日庵　展示期間：11/3～23", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "IV 『君台観左右帳記』の時代"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "日本にもたらされた大陸の文物は、時の権力者によっても重視されるようになり、彼らによって活発にコレクションされるようになります。なかでも足利幕府八代将軍の足利義政が所蔵したとされる「東山御物」と、その飾り方や鑑定に関する指南書である『君台観左右帳記』は、のちの時代の茶の湯のあり方に大きな影響を与えました。そこでは単に中国文化を受容するだけでなく、当時の日本人の価値観による選別のプロセスが働いており、「唐物」というカテゴリーがまさに日本文化現象としてかたちづくられたことが、当時の作品群から見えてきます。本章ではそうした様相を、いわゆる「東山御物」の名品たちを中心に見ることができます。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/10-15.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "国宝　伝閻次平《秋野牧牛図》　中国・南宋時代（13世紀）　泉屋博古館", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/11-14.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "重要文化財　青磁輪花茶碗　銘馬蝗絆　中国・南宋／13世紀　東京国立博物館 Image: TNM image Archive　展示期間：11/25～12/13", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/12-14.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "国宝　玳玻散花文天目茶碗　中国・南宋／12-13世紀　京都・相国寺　展示期間：11/3～23", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "V そして利休へ"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当初は中国文化の強い影響下で形成された喫茶文化は、中世後期になると、徐々に日本独自のものへと変貌を遂げていきます。喫茶の空間を飾る道具たちも、いわゆる「唐物」のみならず、国産の道具が評価を上げていくことになります。「和漢のさかいをまぎらかす」ことが重視されていくわけですが、そうしたなか登場する千利休が、いわゆる「わび茶」の大成者として歴史的に評価されていくことになります。しかし、利休の時代に用いられていた道具を見ていくと、意外にも大陸的要素の強いものがすくなくないことに気づきます。そして、そのなかには中国古代青銅器からの系譜を連綿と受け継ぐデザインも見られるのです。本章では、利休のめざした茶の湯のあり方と、そこに受け継がれる中国古代からの系譜を、名品たちのなかから探っていきます。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/13-8.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "小井戸茶碗　銘六地蔵　朝鮮／16世紀　泉屋博古館東京", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/14-7.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "胡銅桃尻花入　中国・明／15世紀　個人蔵", "credit": "美術展ナビ"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "特集展示 胡銅の鋳造技術をさぐる"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "茶の湯の世界ではもっとも格式の高い、真の花入として重視される胡銅。中国古代青銅器を模したデザインが見られることから、「唐物」としてあつかわれることの多い胡銅ですが、実はその産地については未解明の点が多くのこされています。謎多き胡銅の実態解明をめざして、泉屋博古館は茶道資料館・芦屋釜の里とともに胡銅の鋳造技術の調査を進め、その成果にもとづいて胡銅桃尻花入の鋳造実験にも取り組んできました。この特集展示では実験の成果を公開し、胡銅という「唐物」が誕生する過程について、鋳造技術という観点からせまっていきます。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "絵画・陶磁器・漆工品・金工品など幅広いジャンルから、国宝6点、重要文化財9点を含む約80点が出品（前後期の展示替えあり）される本展。泉屋博古館と茶道資料館（裏千家・今日庵）、芦屋釜の里の三者が結集して、茶の湯デザインの源流に迫っていきます。教科書にも登場する国宝や重要文化財の息をのむ美しさを間近で体感できるだけでなく、最新の鋳造実験によって胡銅の謎に迫るなど、非常に挑戦的な内容となっており、茶の湯ファンはもちろん、東洋美術や工芸愛好家にも見逃せない機会となるはずです。およそ3000年にわたる壮大なデザインの変遷をたどりながら、茶の湯文化の源流をさぐる意欲的な展示を、ぜひ会場で堪能してみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）"}, article_text:
特別展「唐物誕生―茶の湯デザインの源流をさぐる」が泉屋博古館東京（六本木一丁目）で11月3日に開幕しました。会期は12月13日まで。開幕前日の内覧会を取材しました。

いにしえへのあこがれ

中世後期の日本で珍重された舶来の茶道具類「 唐物 」。展示室では、住友コレクションが誇る中国古代青銅器と、いにしえへのあこがれから生み出された工芸品がともに展示され、のちの「唐物」へと受け継がれるデザインの源流が紹介されています。

「東洋のルネサンス」とも称される中国・宋代では、いまから約3000年前の殷・周時代につくられた青銅器に対する関心が急速に高まり、陶磁器や金工品などのデザインにも強く影響をおよぼしました。

展示室では、宋代につくられた殷周時代のデザインを写した作品と、もとになった殷・周時代の作品を同じ空間で鑑賞できます。

作品の中の「音」に注目 徽宗筆の国宝《秋景冬景山水図》など国宝6点

絵画・陶磁器・漆工品・金工品など幅広いジャンルから、国宝6点、重要文化財9点を含む約80点（前後期の展示替えあり）が出品される本展。貴重な作品ばかりですが、特に現存する宋代院体画の傑作に数えられる伝徽宗筆の国宝《秋景冬景山水図》（京都・金地院）が注目です。

描かれているのは、自然の雄大さと厳しさを示す山々と旅人。前期に展示される《秋景山水図》には、木陰に休む人物の視線の先に2羽の鶴を、後期展示の《冬景山水図》には、来た道を振り返る人物の視線の先に、猿を見つけることができます。

画中の人物の視線を追体験するかのような没入感を生む本作。作品の中の「音」を想像して鑑賞してみてください。

「唐物誕生――茶の湯デザインの源流をさぐる」は泉屋博古館東京で12月13日まで。茶の湯の美意識を形作った名品の数々が一堂に会する貴重な機会です。詳しくは下に続くプレビュー記事をご覧ください。 （美術展ナビ編集班・彩）

特別展「唐物誕生―茶の湯デザインの源流をさぐる」

プレビュー記事

泉屋博古館東京（東京都港区）で、「唐物誕生――茶の湯デザインの源流をさぐる」が11月3日から12月13日まで開催されます。

茶の湯デザインの3000年史――中世日本では、大陸との交流のなかで喫茶の風習がもたらされ、やがて「茶の湯」として独自の伝統文化を形成していきます。喫茶に用いられ、そして喫茶の場を彩る道具には「唐物」とよばれる大陸の文物が珍重され、当時の人々の価値観や美意識による選別を経て、いわゆる「名物」として評価されるものも登場しました。

本展ではこうした「唐物」が誕生する過程に焦点が当てられます。はるか中国古代にまでさかのぼって紹介され、胡銅（古銅）とよばれる花入を切り口として、金工品や陶磁器、漆工など、素材を越えた共通性にも着目しながら、茶の湯デザインを東アジア文化史のなかに再定位することが試みられます。さらに、これまで未解明であった胡銅の鋳造技術にせまる特集コーナーも設け、最新の研究成果もあわせて紹介されます。

唐物とは

古代・中世において中国などから輸入された諸物貨に冠せられた和訓の総称（『国史大辞典』）。なかでも日中貿易が盛んになった鎌倉～室町時代には、さまざまな種類の「唐物」がもたらされ、それらはやがて成立してくる茶の湯のなかで貴重な茶道具として珍重されるようになりました。ただし、当時「唐物」と認識されていた文物はかならずしも中国産にはかぎられず、朝鮮半島や東南アジアで制作されたものや、あるいは国産品も含まれます。

本展では中世後期の日本で珍重された舶来の茶道具類を広く「唐物」とよび、中国文物を範としつつ、模倣やアレンジを加えて裾野が広がっていく茶の湯デザインの文化史的背景を、約三千年前の中国古代にまでさかのぼって紹介することが試みられます。

展覧会構成

I いにしえへのあこがれ

いまから約三千年前、殷周時代に盛んにつくられた青銅器は、その造形レベルの高さからのちの時代の美術工芸の模範とされましたが、それだけでなく、周の時代は儒教のなかで理想の治世がなされた時代とされ、その遺風を伝える青銅器は特別に尊ばれるようになりました。「東洋のルネサンス」とも称される宋代では、こうした青銅器に対する関心が急速に高まり、同時代の陶磁器や金工品などのデザインにも強く影響をおよぼすようになります。本章では住友コレクションのほこる中国古代青銅器と、いにしえへのあこがれから生み出された工芸品をともに展示し、のちの「唐物」へと受け継がれるデザインの源流が紹介されます。

II 規範の形成 宋元時代の喫茶文化と文物

宋代以降、士大夫と呼ばれる知識人層が当時の政治・文化の中心をになうようになり、彼らの価値観が強く反映された文物が重視されるようになります。同時に、点茶法とよばれる喫茶も流行し、その用途にかなう道具や、喫茶の空間を飾る工芸品も生み出されました。やがて、こうした文物にあらわされたデザインは、のちの時代まで受け継がれる「規範」を形成し、東アジアの文化に多大な影響を与えるようになります。本章では中国宋元時代の絵画・工芸作品を一堂に会し、この時代の中国で生み出された「古典」とはいかなるものかを探っていきます。

III 日中交易と喫茶文化の伝来

日本中世では、海上交易を通じて大陸との交流が活発におこなわれ、当時の最先端の流行であった喫茶文化にかかわる文物ももたらされることとなりました。それらが日本国内で特に珍重されるようになり、やがて「唐物」として茶の湯の形成に大きな役割を果たします。一方で、単に中国文化に追随するだけでなく、国内でそれを模したもの、そこから日本独自のデザインへと進化したものも生み出されています。本章では日本と大陸の交流の証、そしてメイドインジャパンの胎動を示す作品から、喫茶の受容と文化交流のあり方にせまっていきます。

IV 『君台観左右帳記』の時代

日本にもたらされた大陸の文物は、時の権力者によっても重視されるようになり、彼らによって活発にコレクションされるようになります。なかでも足利幕府八代将軍の足利義政が所蔵したとされる「東山御物」と、その飾り方や鑑定に関する指南書である『君台観左右帳記』は、のちの時代の茶の湯のあり方に大きな影響を与えました。そこでは単に中国文化を受容するだけでなく、当時の日本人の価値観による選別のプロセスが働いており、「唐物」というカテゴリーがまさに日本文化現象としてかたちづくられたことが、当時の作品群から見えてきます。本章ではそうした様相を、いわゆる「東山御物」の名品たちを中心に見ることができます。

V そして利休へ

当初は中国文化の強い影響下で形成された喫茶文化は、中世後期になると、徐々に日本独自のものへと変貌を遂げていきます。喫茶の空間を飾る道具たちも、いわゆる「唐物」のみならず、国産の道具が評価を上げていくことになります。「和漢のさかいをまぎらかす」ことが重視されていくわけですが、そうしたなか登場する千利休が、いわゆる「わび茶」の大成者として歴史的に評価されていくことになります。しかし、利休の時代に用いられていた道具を見ていくと、意外にも大陸的要素の強いものがすくなくないことに気づきます。そして、そのなかには中国古代青銅器からの系譜を連綿と受け継ぐデザインも見られるのです。本章では、利休のめざした茶の湯のあり方と、そこに受け継がれる中国古代からの系譜を、名品たちのなかから探っていきます。

特集展示 胡銅の鋳造技術をさぐる

茶の湯の世界ではもっとも格式の高い、真の花入として重視される胡銅。中国古代青銅器を模したデザインが見られることから、「唐物」としてあつかわれることの多い胡銅ですが、実はその産地については未解明の点が多くのこされています。謎多き胡銅の実態解明をめざして、泉屋博古館は茶道資料館・芦屋釜の里とともに胡銅の鋳造技術の調査を進め、その成果にもとづいて胡銅桃尻花入の鋳造実験にも取り組んできました。この特集展示では実験の成果を公開し、胡銅という「唐物」が誕生する過程について、鋳造技術という観点からせまっていきます。

絵画・陶磁器・漆工品・金工品など幅広いジャンルから、国宝6点、重要文化財9点を含む約80点が出品（前後期の展示替えあり）される本展。泉屋博古館と茶道資料館（裏千家・今日庵）、芦屋釜の里の三者が結集して、茶の湯デザインの源流に迫っていきます。教科書にも登場する国宝や重要文化財の息をのむ美しさを間近で体感できるだけでなく、最新の鋳造実験によって胡銅の謎に迫るなど、非常に挑戦的な内容となっており、茶の湯ファンはもちろん、東洋美術や工芸愛好家にも見逃せない機会となるはずです。およそ3000年にわたる壮大なデザインの変遷をたどりながら、茶の湯文化の源流をさぐる意欲的な展示を、ぜひ会場で堪能してみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

article_text:
Sony Pictures Classics has acquired rights to Niki Byrne’s “ The Julia Set ,” starring Chase Infiniti , following the film’s world premiere at TIFF.

The film, written and directed by Byrne, was one of the festival’s breakouts , thanks in large part to Infiniti’s commanding performance. The “One Battle After Another” and “The Testaments” star earned rave reviews — including in Variety — for her turn as Julia Fischer, a math prodigy navigating being the youngest, most gifted student in her elite prep course, while falling into an abusive romantic relationship with her teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney). Amid those pressures, the film’s synopsis explains, “Julia must find the strength to follow the path she was destined to take.”

Jason Isaacs and Gillian Anderson also star as Pascal’s parents, with Nina Hoss, Carmen Ejogo, Chloe Bailey, Nico Hiraga, Liz Lin and Alex Dillard rounding out the acclaimed cast.

Popular on Variety

“Growing up, I didn’t understand that people made movies. I thought they were the purview of the gods, that they fell out of the sky, and if we were lucky, we caught them,” Byrne said in a statement. “For 35 years, my entire lifetime, Michael Barker, Tom Bernard and their team at Sony Pictures Classics have made sure audiences catch the movies worth catching. I couldn’t be prouder to add ‘The Julia Set’ to their extraordinary library, and to know it will be seen the way movies are meant to be seen: in a darkened theater, together.”

Sony Pictures Classics, led by Michael Barker and Tom Bernard, will distribute the film in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore). The studio is planning a theatrical release next year.

“With subjects as wide-ranging as feminism, romantic infatuation, class differences, familial conflict, bullying and love, and even what it means to be a math prodigy, Niki Byrne’s emotionally engaging and impressive directorial debut gives meaning to living in the modern world,” the Sony Pictures Classics team added.

“Seeing the enthusiastic response at TIFF confirms what promises to be a great theatrical success as well as cements that Chase Infiniti’s much-lauded performance in ‘One Battle After Another’ was no accident,” the studio’s statement continued. “She is at the center of this deeply rich, even suspensefully entertaining film supported by an amazing cast.”

The deal was negotiated between Sony Pictures Classics and Gersh.

article_text:
Pretty in pink: the best of PhotoMonth 2026 – in pictures

This year’s London photography festival takes you from the colourful streets of Kolkata to the grim isolation units of Guantánamo Bay

Thu 15 Oct 2026 02.00 EDT

Kevin You, Encounters 2026, Open Call, Unity and Community

PhotoMonth 26 is at various locations in London until 30 October 2026

Megan Taylor, Siham, from The School Mothers Project, Open Call, Unity and Community
