Source: Adam Rose

Dan Lin

In the latest news in a tumultuous cycle for Netflix, Dan Lin is leaving the streamer nearly three years after he joined as chairman of film.

Netflix confirmed the news on Monday morning. Lin’s departure follows last week’s shuffle that sees Peter Rice replace Bela Bajaria as chief content officer. Rice, who officially starts on October 26, will oversee the film team until a new film head is announced.

Hollywood has undergone huge disruption with industry-wide lay-offs and executive shuffles. The highly-regarded Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy recently left Warner Bros as co-heads of the motion picture group in the wake of the $111bn Skydance merger.

Lin oversaw the release of KPop Demon Hunters , which is the streamer’s most-watched film of all time and won two Oscars this year. Other titles included Animals , 14th , last season’s Oscar nominee Frankenstein , as well as War Machine , Happy Gilmore 2 , The Two Popes , and the upcoming The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth , and 2027 release Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew .

Key acquisitions include Netflix’s top awards contender for this season, La Bola Negra , as well as last year’s Oscar nominated Train Dreams , and Emilia Pérez .

It remains to be seen how the film culture will change at the streamer since it moved away from the higher-quality tastemaker fare championed by Lin’s predecessor, Scott Stuber. Lin was tasked with moving away from high-cost punts on awards bait features involving A-list filmmakers and towards more mainstream fare, organising the film team around distinct genres.

He championed a more robust push into theatrical releases, as seen with last weekend’s release of La Bola Negra and plans for next year’s release of Narnia . However one of Netflix’s challenges has been a slowing down in the rate of viewer engagement in the first half of the year. Among other senior executives on the way out are Lin’s co-head of film Doug Belgrad.

In a statement Lin said, “It’s been a great privilege to lead this incredible team and work with amazing filmmakers and talent to bring their movies to the world. Thank you to Ted, Greg and Bela for the opportunity.”

Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said, “I started working with Dan well before he joined us in 2024 and his strength as a producer was always clear. Once he joined Netflix, I saw up close how his dedication to quality filmmaking, rigour around dealmaking and strategy, and collaborative spirit elevated our film business. I’m grateful to Dan for everything he’s done for Netflix films.”

Netflix is laying off approximately 6% of its workforce in the company’s biggest staff cull. Co-CEOs Sarandos and Greg Peters will join senior executives to report Q3 earnings on Tuesday. Netflix stock dropped a little over 1% on Monday morning and was hovering around $69.57 at time of writing.

Prior to joining Netflix, Lin was founder and CEO of Rideback, and was SVP of Production at Warner Bros, where he served from 1999 to 2007. From 2008 to 2024, films produced by him have grossed more than $6bn at the worldwide box office, including the Lego Movie and Sherlock Holmes franchises, It , and the live-action Disney remakes Lilo & Stitch and Aladdin.

Hochhäuser lösen viele Probleme des Zusammenlebens, sind aber meist nur für wenige zugänglich. Die vielen leerstehenden Bürotürme müssen als öffentlicher Raum neu gedacht werden. Ein Plädoyer für die vertikale Stadt voller Kunst

Jeder in Frankfurt am Main kennt eine Hochhausgeschichte. Oder zumindest jemanden, der eine zu erzählen hat. Meine geht so: Vor vielen Jahren, zur Frankfurter Bahnhofsviertelnacht, hatte einer der schönsten und spektakulärsten Bürotürme der Stadt seine streng bewachten Aufzüge fürs Publikum geöffnet. Die Warteschlangen waren lang. Mit uns nach oben fuhr eine Dame, die hier offenbar noch zu Deutsche-Bank-Zeiten als Sekretärin gearbeitet hatte: "Nach Feierabend immer ins Schwimmbad, 31. Etage!"

In jenem Fahrstuhl kletterte zu einer mutmaßlich ähnlichen Zeit auch der Schauspieler Götz George durch den hessischen Silberturm, als arroganter Werbemanager Jörg, der im TV-Thriller "Abwärts" zwischen den Etagen steckenbleibt und sich schweißgebadet freikämpft. Eine Symbolik von oben und unten, wie man sie heute in den fiesesten Banker-Dystopien nicht mehr so schön inszeniert findet.

Diese Geschichte erzählte ich neulich, als wir entlang der Fast-Wolkenkratzer am Main wanderten und uns wunderten, wer oder was da eigentlich zu Hause ist. Ihre Schatten werfen die Bauten über ganze Stadtviertel (und heizen sie mit ihren Glasfassaden weiter auf), aber drin war man allenfalls bis zur fünften Etage. "Oben bleiben!", heißt es nicht umsonst für die happy few, und dazu passen die Bilder von den Pissoirs eines großen deutschen Banktowers, von wo aus die Vorstandsetage sinnbildlich auf die unter ihnen liegende Stadt pinkeln kann.

Lösungen für alle möglichen Probleme

Nichts gegen den Bautypus an sich: Hochhäuser sind eine fantastische Idee. Auf geringer Grundfläche bieten sie theoretisch Lösungen für alle möglichen Platzprobleme im urbanen Zusammenleben. In den europäischen Nachbarländern wird ohnehin viel öfter in die Höhe gebaut – in Holland gibt es kaum eine Mittelstadt, die nicht rund um die Bahnhöfe Wohntürme nebeneinandersetzt. In Helsinki zählten die innerstädtischen Mehrfamilienhäuser schon vor 100 Jahren oft nicht drei, sondern fünf oder sechs Etagen. Und erinnert sich noch irgendjemand unter 30 daran, dass es in New York City in den Türmen des World Trade Centers seinerzeit ein eigenes Residency-Programm für Kunstschaffende gab, städtisch gefördert und bis zum Terroranschlag vom 11. September 2001 voll genutzt?

Die Verhältnisse sind in Deutschland anders, zumal in der Stadt Frankfurt, die sich zu Recht viel auf ihre Skyline einbildet. Künstlerinnen und Künstler erhalten allenfalls ab und zu im Rahmen einer Audienz Zugang – wenn eine Anwaltskanzlei zum Meet-and-Greet lädt, beispielsweise. Auch deshalb knallen die seltenen Kunstausstellungen in entsprechender Höhe umso mehr.

Unvergessen ist die von Frankfurter Künstlern auf klandestinem Wege organisierte Schau "Orbit" , mit der Arthur Loewen und Béla Feldberg zu Corona-Zeiten eine ganze ehemalige Büro-Etage im Messeturm bespielten. Die Salon-Kunstmesse House of Galleries lädt im Januar 2027 zur zeitweiligen Reaktivierung des Trianon-Hochhauses in Form der vermutlich höchsten Kunstmesse der Gegenwart. Man kann sie auch als Blaupause für das verstehen, was möglich wäre.

Staubsaugen im leeren Drittwohnsitz

Für die übrige Zeit bleibt man eher unten. Da ist es inzwischen kalt geworden. Während wir über fehlenden Atelierraum und den Mangel an Freiräumen jenseits der Institutionen sprechen, fällt mir eine weitere Geschichte ein: Die eines Mieters, der in einem jener Luxustürme im Europaviertel wohnt und sich gelegentlich etwas gruselt, weil er abends ganz allein auf der Etage ist. Nachbarn aus Fleisch und Blut gibt es kaum. Rundherum vor allem Zweit- oder Drittwohnsitze.

Tagsüber kommen regelmäßig die Reinigungstrupps, um die leerstehenden Investitionsbehausungen staubzusaugen. Da liegen Assoziationen an die Serie "Station Eleven" nahe, in der die Apokalypse in einem Wohnturm in Chicago ausbricht und die Verhältnisse rasch ziemlich prekär werden. Der Schlüssel läge hier wohl in einer erheblichen Zweitwohnsitzsteuer oder der Bevorzugung von Erstwohnsitzen für die Bürger einer Region.

Oft wird über die Gestaltung des öffentlichen Raums gesprochen – aber wenig bis gar nicht über die vertikale Stadt, in der rein privat über Zugang entschieden wird. Man stelle sich vor, hunderte Meter Straßenzüge auf dem Boden blieben für die Öffentlichkeit dauerhaft unzugänglich: Die lebhafte Debatte wäre programmiert.

Ganze Häuser stehen leer

In die Höhe geschraubt wird die Exklusivität jedoch wie selbstverständlich akzeptiert. Dabei stehen inmitten der Skyline nicht nur einzelne Etagen, sondern teils ganze Gebäude leer (in Frankfurt am Main sind das je nach Schätzung zwischen 11 und 14 Prozent der Fläche, Tendenz steigend). Während neue, energieeffiziente Hochhäuser schon weit vor Fertigstellung vermietet sind, fristen die älteren Bauwerke ein schwieriges Dasein. Sicherheitsanforderungen sind hoch, eine Umnutzung ist nicht ohne Weiteres rentabel.

Im Deutschen Architekturmuseum in Framkfurt am Main findet passend zu diesen Überlegungen gerade eine kleine Ausstellung statt. "Aufmachen! Rethinking High-Rises" ist sie kämpferisch überschrieben. Zu sehen gibt es radikale Ideen und Beispiele von erfolgreichem Umdenken.

Manchmal wird der vorhandene Raum dabei erweitert: Der Centre Point Tower in London, Jahrgang 1966, wurde beispielsweise von einem Bürohochhaus in ein Wohngebäude mit Einzelhandel, Gastronomie und öffentlich zugänglichen Räumen im Erdgeschoss umgestaltet. Ein weitgehend ungenutztes Hochhaus aus den 1990er-Jahren im chinesischen Shenzhen ist heute ein Zentrum für Frauen und Kinder, das mit seiner farbenprächtigen Fassade schon von Weitem Freundlichkeit statt Kühle ausstrahlen soll. Und der historische Book Tower in Detroit, 1926 nach Plänen von Louis Kamper erbaut, ist heute ein Vorbild für die Mischnutzung mit Wohnraum, Büros, Hotel und Einzelhandel, darunter Cafés und Kunstgalerien.

Eurotowers zu Kulturflächen

Auch für Frankfurt hat die Ausstellung einige Vorschläge parat, zusätzlich zu den bereits bestehenden erfolgreichen Umnutzungen (wie einem kompletten Umbau eines Bürohochhauses aus den 1960er-Jahren in Niederrad): Der Sockel des seit Jahren leerstehenden Eurotowers könnte entkernt und als offene Kultur- oder Gastronomiefläche wieder zur Stadt geöffnet werden. Die alte Zentrale der Landesbank Hessen-Thüringen könnte durch Dachgärten und vertikale Bepflanzung mehr Grün in die kommenden Hitzesommer bringen.

Dem Plädoyer der Ausstellung kann man sich nur anschließen: Hochhäuser zu Gärten, zu Ateliers, zu Proberäumen! Und bitte auch zu Wohnraum, der wirklich bewohnt wird. Dazu bräuchte es zunächst nicht einmal eine architektonische Umgestaltung, sondern als Allererstes politischen Gestaltungswillen.

article_text:
Die Ökumenische Jury zeichnet beim 42. Film Festival in Warschau den Film „The Child“ von Linda Olte aus. Darin geht es um ein kinderloses Paar, das auf unterschiedliche Weise mit dem nicht in Erfüllung gehenden Kinderwunsch umgeht.

Das Internationale Filmfestival in Warschau (8.10.-18.10.2026) feierte in diesem Jahr seine 42. Ausgabe. Die Ökumenische Jury verlieh ihren Preis an den Film „ The Child “ von der lettischen Regisseurin Linda Olte. Der Film erzählt von einem Paar, das sich seit mehr als zehn Jahren vergeblich ein Kind wünscht und dafür schon zahlreiche Wege zur Erfüllung seines Wunsches ausprobiert hat. Während der Mann in der Beziehung allmählich akzeptiert, dass man auch ein erfülltes Leben ohne Nachkommen führen kann, kann sich seine Frau mit dem Gedanken nicht abfinden, niemals eine Mutter zu werden.

In der Begründung der dreiköpfigen Jury heißt es, dass das Drama eines der sensibelsten Themen menschlicher Existenz anspreche: „Ein Kind zu haben und eine Familie zu gründen, ist der Wunsch vieler Menschen. Wenn ein Paar daran scheitert, sich diesen Wunsch zu erfüllen, stürzt es in eine tiefe Krise. Das Vertrauen in sich selbst und in den anderen wird auf eine harte Probe gestellt.“ Neben den wichtigen ethischen Fragen, die die lettisch-litauische Produktion zu diesem Thema aufgreife, wird vor allem die kinematografische Sprache gelobt, die die komplexen Gefühle der Figuren „kühn und doch zart“ zum Ausdruck bringe. Gleichzeitig führen die inneren Konflikte die Figuren des Filmes dahin, „einen neuen Lebenssinn zu finden, der ihnen Erfüllung und Hoffnung bringt.“

Mitglieder der Ökumenischen Jury waren Marciej Franciszczak als Jurypräsident sowie Margrit Frölich und Carlos Minondo.

Neben dem Gewinner der ökumenischen Jury wurden auch andere Filme bei dem osteuropäischen Filmfestival ausgezeichnet: Den Warschauer „Grand Prix“ gewann „ Cudze Rzeczy “ (What Belongs to Others) von Grzegorz Dębowski. Der Preis für die beste Regie ging an Caj Chengjie für seinen Film „ Suzhou Quartet “. Den Preis der Jury der internationalen Filmkritik („Fipresci“) erhielt „ Przez ścianę “ (Through the Wall) von Maciej Sobieszczański. Eröffnet wurde das Festival am 9. Oktober von dem norwegisch-dänischen Spielfilm „ Growth of the Soil " von Hans Petter Moland.

article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2025 Fantasia coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 23.

We enter Steve Pink’s Terrestrial with a tour through an opulent home––broken glass on the floor, a blood trail towards the door, and Allen (Jermaine Fowler) sat against the wall in a frozen panic. Before we can even begin to presume what might have occurred, however, we’re whisked to a car inhabited by three of his old college friends: Maddie (Pauline Chalamet), Ryan (James Morosini), and Vic (Edy Modica). En route to see Allen for the first time in years, they’re worried about the state in which they might find him. His mother called in a fright about him potentially being suicidal, so it’s more than a little surprising when he greets them outside his giant mansion with joy.

Our assumption is thus that Samuel Johnson and Connor Diedrich’s script is teasing us with a possible future. A glimpse of what might arise once the façade of Allen’s happiness makes way for the truth of his hidden sorrow. It makes sense until we learn more about the television show playing on a loop inside a room dedicated to its literary and cinematic history. Allen is a huge fan of The Neptune Cycle and relates to its alien race spying on Earth to discover an unlikely hero to take back home. What starts as him gushing about his passion soon gives way to a strange defensiveness, though. Weirder still are Allen’s odd mannerisms and mood swings. Perhaps that opening actually revealed the past.

This is a genre film taking big narrative and tonal swings, so the chance Allen is walking himself off a cliff of lies to a bloody end is just as likely as him being chosen and replaced by an alien at a moment of desperate need. It’s a question that lingers for the entire first act––Allen is truly making the wildest decisions. He tells Vic he made breakfast the next morning, only for her to find a plate of pickles and string cheese in the kitchen. That’s some extraterrestrial-pretending-to-be-human nonsense if I’ve ever seen it. Pair that with a short fuse morphing back into a smile as fast as it turned to rage, and body-snatching seems reasonable. Until the first of many new discoveries changes everything.

It’s a reveal that provides an answer to our original question while introducing many more upon rewinding for the additional context we never fathomed needing. The result is an even darker tale. Allen is still drowning, but the water is deeper than merely depression. No, he’s gone and put himself into a situation that was fully outside his control from the get-go and only seems to grow worse with every passing minute. What began as a victimless crime quickly transforms into a full-blown hostage situation, more and more characters coming out of the woodwork to chip away at what little sanity Allen had left. Once that’s gone, the line separating reality and fiction disappears altogether.

Pink amplifies this fractured psychosis by splicing in scenes of the show that mimic what’s happening to Allen. That means spending time with the crudely vintage sci-fi antics of Taylor Gray and Violet Beane on a CRT screen as they traverse the cosmos under the stewardship of the Voxxxti (the director’s Hot Tub Time Machine pals Craig Robinson and Rob Corddry also make appearances). Think of it as a defense mechanism. When things go wrong, Allen’s only way to keep from breaking down is to filter things through this fictional lens. Death becomes an illusion. Crimes become necessity. Neptune Cycle creator SJ Purcell (Brendan Hunt) would be proud if he didn’t have his own problems.

Terrestrial wears a pitch-black humor on its sleeve, a fact that won’t prepare you for how bleak the filmmakers are willing to run. Right when you think things are falling apart perfectly for Allen to ease out of trouble (or, at the very least, mitigate it so his friends can escape) Pink and company hit the gas and ensure the consequences of his actions land as hard and painful as possible. I love the willingness to go for the jugular and really push this character to a point of no return as far as being unable to accept what he has wrought. It provides Fowler a great acting showcase, demanding he constantly flip between devastation and an uncanny calm. The death of a dream can sometimes be impossible to bear.

Hunt adds some welcome deadpan to the proceedings as Purcell’s issues merge with Allen’s, lending the right amount of drama to contrast the otherwise absurdist nature of Fowler’s off-putting hosting style. Modica injects broader humor, Rob Yang brings an unnaturally pleasant air of danger, and Morosini and Chalamet supply an uncertainty to feed Allen’s derangement. The script proposes multiple ways out just a moment too late, thus increasing the cost of Allen’s recklessness––his only real exit returns to that initial choice between death and abduction. But it’s no longer a choice; the former’s inevitability ultimately renders the latter essential.

Terrestrial premiered at the 2025 Fantasia International Film Festival.

article_text:
A24 ’s “ You Can See Everything ” has become one of the year’s biggest box office surprises, opening to a staggering $15.6 million in the U.S. and generating a frenzy of headlines, spoilers, memes and online chatter. But for audiences outside North America, catching Nathan Fielder’s three-hour documentary about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes — now expected to be a major player in awards season — has become a waiting game.

Despite the film’s blockbuster debut — the second-biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary, behind “Fahrenheit 9/11” — A24 isn’t releasing it in the U.K. and Australia until Nov. 20, more than a month after its U.S. bow. Sony Pictures, which recently acquired the film for several international territories, including Germany, Latin America and South Korea, has yet to announce its release plans.

Related Stories

Atlanta Hawks Strike Streaming Alliance With Amazon's Prime Video

Park Min-young, Yook Sung-jae, Go Soo Lead Prime Video Korean Office Romance 'Nine to Six'

As one producer jokingly put it in a message to Variety : “You Can See Everything, unless you live outside N. America.”

The frustration was palpable at the BFI London Film Festival, where excited speculation was mounting that the documentary would be unveiled as the surprise screening on Oct. 16. With co-director Lance Oppenheim in town earlier that week (for his other film, “Primetime”) and a special BAFTA screening having taken place that afternoon, many festivalgoers were convinced “You Can See Everything” was heading to the Royal Festival Hall.

Instead, the surprise screening turned out to be Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky.”

The delay raises a broader question about A24’s international release strategy at a time when social media can turn a film into a global cultural event overnight. Because “You Can See Everything” isn’t alone among the studio’s titles that make non-U.S. audiences sit tight, something that has been widely lamented online.

Oppenheim’s Robert Pattinson starring “Primetime” released in the U.S. on Sep. 25, becoming A24’s third biggest opening with $19.2 million after “Backrooms” and “Civil War.” U.K. previews kick off on Oct. 28, just days before it gets VOD launch in the U.S. (like “You Can See Everything,” Sony picked up the film for numerous other territories). Back in 2022, A24’s megahit and Oscar winner “Everything Everywhere All at Once” released in the U.K. a full two months after bowing in the U.S. And then there’s another of 2026’s most hotly-anticipated titles, “Club Kid,” which is suffering a similar fate. Jordan Firstman’s acclaimed directorial debut and Cannes breakout lands in cinemas in the U.S on Nov. 6. In the U.K.? Jan. 8, 2027.

There are, of course, several factors at play. A24 — which wouldn’t comment on its release strategy for this article — only self-distributes outside North America in a couple of territories, notably the U.K./Ireland and Australia/New Zealand, and even then many of its titles go through a third party (the films named above were all handled solely by A24). There’s also the long-held sense that having an advanced U.S. campaign is extremely beneficial to help test the waters and serve as a momentum-building ice-breaker for the overseas trip.

“But for a film that is so spoiler-heavy as ‘You Can See Everything,’ a month is extraordinary,” notes one Brit doc publicity veteran. It should be noted that last Christmas’ extremely buzzy A24 release “Marty Supreme” came out in the U.K. less than a week after the U.S. and grossed in excess of $22 million, the studio’s biggest success on British shores to date.

But perhaps “You Can See Everything” is a very unique case. After all, very few people outside of the inner A24-Fielder-Oppenheim circle knew anything about it before its shock Telluride screening. As one insider notes, “The film really didn’t exist in the world until six weeks ago.” A24 has had a tight turnaround to get it into U.S. cinemas since then. Perhaps a simultaneous or near-simultaneous launch in the U.K. — where it has an office overseeing local productions but no dedicated distribution team — was a step too far (especially given it’s gearing up to release “Primetime” as well).

There’s also the possibility that simply few expected “You Can See Everything” — a documentary almost as long as “Oppenheimer” and about a disgraced and overexposed Silicon Valley founder who has already been the center of a hit TV drama — to become such a theatrical juggernaut. Was the power of Fielder and this stunt release underestimated?

Not so — at least not among those who know documentaries — claims the publicity vet.

“Within the very rarefied documentary world, the minute it was announced, everyone knew it was going be huge,” they say. “Maybe A24 isn’t plugged in as much, but as soon as Elizabeth Holmes’ face popped up, everyone was just like, ‘Well that’s just blown ‘NAZA’ out.'”

In terms of timing, to launch in the U.K. on the same date as the U.S. would have seen “You Can See Everything” go up against fellow new releases in the video game adaptation “Streetfighter” and animated feature “Forgotten Island” (and not, unlike America, the closest potential rival in terms of audiences, “Sense & Sensibility”). That said, the U.K. is about to go into school half-term holidays, not generally suited, at least when it comes to more mainstream-focused cinemas, for arthouse-focused indies.

“If someone had tried to get us to put a 3-hour doc in our cinemas just ahead of half term, we probably wouldn’t have even answered their calls,” says one exhibition exec, who admits his audiences tend to lean much more towards the popcorn titles. “This is just the wrong type and shape of film for us during that period, which is more horror classics and family fun.” The exec suggests that a post-holiday early November release might have been more strategic, but then that would put “You Can See Everything” firmly on the heels of “Primetime.”

One U.K. industry insider also suggests that A24 may have actually tried to sell “You Can See Everything,” but in the U.K., a theatrical market where indie films are increasingly struggling to find a foothold, couldn’t find a distributor willing to pay the price (at least not before its dramatic U.S. unveiling). “So it may have been simpler for them to release themselves,” they say. “And hats of them — the U.S. release has really shown the value of the film.”

Whatever the factor — or numerous factors — behind it, a month-long wait to see a film the entire internet appears to be talking about (and avoid the numerous spoiler-filled articles and posts along the way) will likely be an excruciating experience for many. But it does appear to have done wonders for pre-sales.

According to a report in The Guardian earlier this week, tickets at London’s Picturehouse Central cinema went on sale before its U.S. opening, with the demand forcing the chain to put on additional screenings. It was a similar situation at Cineworld, which has added more screenings at its major Leicester Square site and expanded bookings elsewhere after the initial batch of tickets sold out.

Variety has since heard that Australia’s Palace Cinemas — which operates in 25 locations across the country — has just broken the record for single-day pre-sales with “You Can See Everything.” Such was the demand for tickets for Fielder’s wild, genre-flipping documentary that sales doubled that of the previous record holder: “Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour.”

article_text:
MUBI renueva su catálogo en noviembre con grandes historias, cine de autor y títulos imperdibles como The Curse y Making Marie Antoinette .

MUBI anunció sus estrenos de noviembre de 2026 con una programación que combina cine de autor, documentales, series y colecciones especiales. Entre las principales novedades se destacan Making Marie Antoinette , el documental de Eleanor Coppola sobre el detrás de cámaras de la película de su hija Sofia Coppola; The Curse , la irreverente serie creada por Nathan Fielder y Benny Safdie, con Emma Stone como protagonista; y El deshielo , de Manuela Martelli, seleccionada por Chile para competir por el Oscar 2027.

La programación también incluye Love Letters , ópera prima de Alice Douard sobre el amor y la maternidad; Músicas , el documental de Lila Avilés; y Taxi Moto , de Gaël Kamilindi. A su vez, la plataforma presentará colecciones dedicadas al cine surcoreano, las comedias de Quentin Dupieux, el policial y el cine contemporáneo internacional, además de la reconocida Trilogía de la luz , del realizador chileno Patricio Guzmán.

3 de noviembre

Persecución: thrillers de asesinos de Corea del Sur: la colección incluye Train to Busan , de Yeon Sang-ho, donde un padre y su hija deben luchar por sobrevivir cuando un brote zombi desata el caos dentro de un tren.

5 de noviembre

FICUNAM: Cruzar el umbral: una selección de cinco propuestas del cine contemporáneo internacional que exploran la memoria, la política, las relaciones humanas y el medioambiente. Entre los títulos se encuentran Rolle Workshop, a Journey , The Lake , El león , Elegy for the Forgotten , On an Endless War y Un río y una reina .

6 de noviembre

Making Marie Antoinette: Eleanor Coppola registra el rodaje de la película de su hija, Sofia Coppola, y ofrece una mirada íntima al proceso creativo de la cineasta, así como a la relación entre ambas.

Te puede interesar

Streaming: 3 películas para mirar este fin de semana

Los títulos para disfrutar este fin de semana en streaming

Aventura alocada: las comedias de Quentin Dupieux: la colección reúne el humor absurdo del realizador francés. Uno de sus títulos destacados es Fumar causa tos , protagonizada por un grupo de justicieros que debe recuperar la cohesión de su equipo tras enfrentarse a una tortuga demoníaca.

13 de noviembre

Love Letters: la primera película de Alice Douard sigue a Céline y Nadia, una pareja que espera a su primera hija. Mientras se prepara para la maternidad, Céline debe enfrentarse a un sistema burocrático que no reconoce plenamente su lugar en la vida de la niña.

El deshielo: dirigida por Manuela Martelli, la película reconstruye los secretos familiares y las heridas de Chile tras la dictadura militar a partir de la desaparición de una joven esquiadora alemana.

Músicas: el documental de Lila Avilés acompaña a Mujeres del Viento Florido, una banda filarmónica femenina integrada por mujeres de comunidades indígenas mexicanas. Su recorrido celebra la identidad cultural y la resistencia a través de la música.

19 de noviembre

The Curse: creada por Nathan Fielder y Benny Safdie, la serie combina sátira social, humor incómodo y suspenso. Emma Stone, Fielder y Safdie protagonizan la historia de un matrimonio que intenta desarrollar un proyecto inmobiliario sustentable mientras graba un reality, en medio de acusaciones de gentrificación y una supuesta maldición que amenaza su relación.

20 de noviembre

Wanted!: películas policiales: la colección incorpora The Crimson Rivers , thriller dirigido por Mathieu Kassovitz. La investigación de un brutal asesinato conduce a dos policías por un entramado de secretos, conspiraciones y privilegios.

27 de noviembre

Taxi Moto: el cortometraje dirigido y protagonizado por Gaël Kamilindi sigue a un cineasta que debe replantear su película sobre una historia de amor entre dos hombres debido a las restricciones de su país de origen. La propuesta aborda la censura y la libertad creativa.

Trilogía de la luz: MUBI reúne tres documentales fundamentales de Patricio Guzmán sobre la memoria y la historia chilena: Nostalgia de la luz , que conecta la astronomía con la búsqueda de desaparecidos durante la dictadura; El botón de nácar , que recupera las voces de los pueblos indígenas a través del agua; y La cordillera de los sueños , donde los Andes funcionan como testigos de las heridas políticas del país.

article_text:
Skydance , as it embarks on the work to integrate the businesses of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, is offering certain employees a voluntary buyout in a “one-time offer.”

The new program was outlined by chairman and CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz in a memo to staffers Monday.

“As we bring our teams together, we recognize that not everyone will see their future here, and we respect that. To give eligible employees the option to move on in a way that works for them, we are introducing a Voluntary Buyout (VBO) Program,” the execs wrote. “Those who qualify will receive an individual communication with their personalized details and terms, and a window to decide whether to accept this one-time offer.”

Related Stories

France's Luxbox, Spain’s Amore Cine Join Melina León's Ventana Sur Proyecta Title ‘Portrait Huaco’ (EXCLUSIVE)

Ventana Sur Proyecta 2026: A Powerhouse New Generation Lineup Backed by Some of Latin America’s Finest Producers

They added, “Please know we don’t take any of this lightly. We are clear about what we’re building: a company that tells the stories people around the world love, embraces new ways to connect with audiences, and leads the next era of media and entertainment. We have the talent, the creative firepower and the ambition to do it, and we will get there together.”

Paramount’s massive $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery closed on Oct. 6. In their “Day One” memo to employees that day, Ellison and Kreiz (who was the CEO of Mattel before joining the new Skydance earlier this month) acknowledged that layoffs will be part of the process. “Integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce,” the execs wrote in that memo. “We are committed to handling this process thoughtfully and respectfully.”

In the Oct. 26 memo, Ellison and Kreiz also said the new Skydance is moving to a mandatory five-days-per-week in-office policy across the company. “We believe in-person collaboration is vital to our culture and to the success of our business. Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems,” the execs said. “We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We’ve seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them.”

Skydance execs have said they are shooting to achieve more than $6 billion in cost savings on an annualized basis within three years, and part of that will come from layoffs. The company has not revealed at this point the extent of the job cuts it expects. According to a report issued by Los Angeles County in August, the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger could result in the loss of some 4,500 film and TV jobs over three years in L.A. alone.

Read the full memo sent by Skydance’s top brass Monday, a copy of which was obtained by Variety :

Team,

At Skydance, our goal is to build the next-generation media and entertainment company, powered by creativity and technology. We are creative-first, audience focused, tech-forward and globally scaled. And in a world of endless choice and fierce competition for attention, we don’t just want to succeed. We want to win.

To do that, we must be a strong, connected and agile company. Among our business and creative priorities, none matters more than building a strong culture, because it’s the foundation of everything we want to achieve. Winning requires us to work as one team: one company, fully aligned. That means communicating openly and collaborating efficiently across every part of the organization.

In-Person Collaboration

We believe in-person collaboration is vital to our culture and to the success of our business. Especially in a creative company like ours, the best ideas come from people in the same room, sharing perspectives, challenging one another and solving problems. Being together isn’t just about showing up. It’s about inspiring one another, learning and coaching, forming friendships and having the casual conversations that spark something great.

With that in mind, we will adopt a five-day in-office policy across all of Skydance. We truly believe this is in the best interest of our company and our people. We’ve seen the benefits firsthand at Paramount, and we want every part of Skydance to share in them.

While many of you are already in the office five days a week, we understand this may be a significant change to the daily routines of others. To give you time to plan and adjust, we will take a phased approach by location. You will receive ample notice before changes take effect, and we will work closely with managers to support you through the transition.

Voluntary Buyout Program

As we bring our teams together, we recognize that not everyone will see their future here, and we respect that. To give eligible employees the option to move on in a way that works for them, we are introducing a Voluntary Buyout (VBO) Program. Those who qualify will receive an individual communication with their personalized details and terms, and a window to decide whether to accept this one-time offer.

We recognize this is a significant decision, and we want you to feel informed and supported. If this applies to you, please review your materials carefully and reach out to your leadership or HR representative with any questions. FAQs and other resources are available on the Skydance Integration Hub, and HR support is also available through My Paramount (legacy Paramount employees) or Ask Employee Connection on WBD One (legacy Warner Bros. employees).

Please know we don’t take any of this lightly. We are clear about what we’re building: a company that tells the stories people around the world love, embraces new ways to connect with audiences, and leads the next era of media and entertainment. We have the talent, the creative firepower and the ambition to do it, and we will get there together.

Thank you for your commitment, and for the creativity and passion you bring to your work every day.

Best,

David and Ynon

We wanted to capture the essence of Stallone."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“As good as this script was, if you had a different actor, we wouldn’t be sitting here. Source: Rome Film Fest

Anthony Ippolito and Peter Farrelly at Rome Film Fest

Speaking at the Rome Film Fest press conference for Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky , Anthony Ippolito described the “weight of the responsibility” of playing a young Sylvester Stallone, and a physically gruelling shoot that left him ill by its final days.

“There was a lot of intimidation at the beginning,” said Ippolito, who is also in Rome to receive the festival’s Progressive Award, which honours promising careers in the making.

“I was a fan of the movies and a fan of the character, and I understand how many people are, so I did feel the weight of the responsibility. But like any other situation, you just start by researching as much as you can.”

I Play Rocky charts the making of 1976’s Rocky , which a then-unknown Stallone wrote and refused to sell unless he could play the lead. The film also stars Stephan James as Carl Weathers, Matt Dillon as Stallone’s father and Jay Duplass as director John G. Avildsen.

Ippolito transformed his body and modelled his performance to mimic the personality and voice of a young Stallone, who was yet to turn 30 when Rocky was made and had grown up inspired by bodybuilder-turned-actor Steve Reeves, building his physique from a young age while living with facial paralysis.

“I don’t want to say as a compensation for the paralysis, but it was a very interesting and necessary part of the character,” said Ippolito, who also gained “a considerable amount of weight” for the role.

Casting

According to Farrelly, also participating in the Rome press conference, Ippolito landed the breakout role after sending in a self-tape audition tape performing scenes from the script. “He was the first person we looked at, the only person,” said the director. “When I saw it, I said, ‘That’s it, search is over.’ I didn’t care if he’d ever been in anything else.”

Only later, during pre-production, did Farrelly discover that Ippolito had previously played a young Al Pacino in Paramount+ series The Offer , about the making of The Godfather .

Asked about the recent trend for actors to replicate real-life figures as exactly as possible, Farrelly said impressions alone were not enough. “A lot of people have done impressions of Stallone. Jim Carrey does an amazing one, but it’s not real. We wanted to capture the essence of Stallone.

“As good as this script was, if you had a different actor, we wouldn’t be sitting here. We’re here because he became Stallone,” added Farrelly.

Ippolito, who spent more than a year studying Stallone’s interviews online and comparing them with Rocky, pointed out that Stallone’s vocal and physical mannerisms had to be replicated because it is part of the plot. “The studio wanted all these other actors, celebrities at the time, because he didn’t look and talk like a movie star,” he said.

About a month before shooting, Ippolito finally got the chance to speak to Stallone, and described him as “very open and generous [about] what it was like to be in those rooms with the producers, and before that, when he was really down and out”.

“He did feel very much like a lone wolf, kind of like an orphan in life in a lot of ways,” added Ippolito. “He had so much going against him and he persevered through so much. His endurance, I think, radiates through Rocky .”

Test of endurance

I Play Rocky ’s production mirrored the original’s struggles, according to Farrelly: “They shot Rocky in 28 days. We shot this in 34 days. That’s tight.”

For Ippolito, the shoot became his own test of endurance. Scenes shot in cold warehouses in New Jersey and Philadelphia in November, while being repeatedly sprayed down with fake sweat, left him “pretty sick” by the end.

“It was a very emotional shoot, and taxing in that way, but also very physically taxing,” he said.

I Play Rocky is produced by Toby Emmerich, Christian Baha, Farrelly, Paul Currie and Michele Weiss. It was runner-up for the People’s Choice Award at Toronto, and screens in Rome’s Grand Public section.

Amazon MGM Studios releases the film in select US cinemas on November 6, and Eagle Pictures opens it in Italy on December 31.
